That opinion rejected one argument the President had raised for federalization; today’s decision in California’s case also rejects the President’s made-up assertion that there was a “rebellion” in Los Angeles that warranted federalizing the Guard, which the court held was not “a colorable assessment within a ‘range of honest judgment.’”

Today’s rejection of Trump’s “rebellion” claim is a critical safeguard ahead of next month’s elections: Donald Trump is on notice that the courts will swat down any false claims of emergencies and rebellions to militarize our communities, intimidate citizens, and engage in authoritarian tactics.

The fight for upholding the Constitution

In June 2025, following President Trump’s call to arrest Governor Gavin Newsom, Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit on behalf of Governor Gavin Newsom against the Trump administration to end the illegal and unnecessary takeover of a CalGuard unit, which needlessly escalated chaos and violence in the Los Angeles region.

Under the California Constitution, Governor Newsom is the Commander-in-Chief of the California National Guard. In the lawsuit, Governor Newsom and Attorney General Bonta explained that the federal government overstepped its legal authority and bypassed the Governor’s approval to take over a unit of CalGuard, in a situation where federal government intervention was not needed and did not meet the necessary criteria for federalization. text:
Fewer people became U.S. citizens in recent months compared to the past two years, with a group representing naturalized immigrants raising concerns that the Trump administration is actively suppressing new voters just days before the midterms.

Newsweek analysis of naturalization data showed approvals fell to around 57,700 during the third quarter of Fiscal Year 2026, compared to over 200,000 in the same periods in 2024 and 2025, while pending cases soared above 742,000, according to the latest data from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

Citizenship grants the right to vote in federal elections, with the latest figures prompting concern from the National Partnership for New Americans (NPNA) that a deliberate effort was underway to prevent new voter registrations.

Read More on Politics

"When I looked at the data, I just see a swift denial of, or negation of, processing applications and so we can ascertain that it's part of a strategy to cull or to limit people's access to naturalization and therefore civic engagement," Nicole Melaku, the executive director of the NPNA, told Newsweek. "In another political reality and in other administrations, you would not see that many applications pending and just sitting in a backlog."

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek it had changed its policy from the "rubber-stamping" under the Biden administration.

Drop in Naturalizations: What the Data Shows

USCIS released its latest quarterly data on applications, running April through June 2026, in late September, showing a growing backlog of citizenship applications.

Newsweek compared Quarter 3 data for 2026 with the previous two years. The 2024 data fell under President Joe Biden, while the 2025 data belongs to the current Trump administration.

Two years ago, 218,720 applications for naturalization were approved by USCIS, with 462,974 pending. The numbers rose in 2025 to 241,326 approvals and 529,018 pending. By 2026, the approval rate dropped significantly to 57,697, while the number of applications waiting rose again to 742,138.

The biggest drops in approvals were seen in largely Democrat-leaning or large metropolitan areas.

At the San Jose, California, field office, 317 cases were approved April-June this year, compared to 9,041 in 2025—a 96.5 percent drop. In Seattle, Washington, approvals fell 90.3 percent year-on-year, while in Houston, cases were down just shy of 50 percent.

Across the U.S., naturalization approvals fell in 2026, but some of the biggest drops came in the states that tend to have higher numbers of immigrants—California, New York, Florida, and Texas, which often have the highest numbers of naturalized citizens.

Several of the states affected are places where naturalized voters make up a substantial share of the electorate.

According to Pew Research Center in 2024, 55 percent of naturalized voters lived in Florida, Texas, California, and New York. In 13 states and Washington, D.C., naturalized citizens made up around 10 percent or more of the number of eligible voters.

"Vast numbers of people in blue cities, and in what we call gateway cities with large numbers of immigrants, are just sitting there without being processed," Melaku said. "You look in Philly, 17,000 applications. In Houston, 31,000 applications pending. We have Georgia, 17,300 applications just pending.

"So you look at the volatility in those particular markets or parts of the country, and you could pretty much see that they're dragging their feet on processing these applications and making sure that these people will be stuck in either a backlog and or a never-ending adjudication with no clear timeline on when they can finally take their oath of citizenship."

Are New Voters Being Kept From the Midterms?

Delays and backlogs in immigration application processing are nothing new, but attorneys and advocates have been raising concerns over the past 19 months that Trump administration policies have made the situation worse.

Adam Klein, a former senior DHS official and co-founder of Globali.ai, told Newsweek that during his time with USCIS, similar concerns about backlogs were raised.

"During the first Trump administration, there were concerns that the threatened furlough of thousands of USCIS employees in 2020 could slow naturalizations ahead of the election," Klein said, explaining that furloughs were canceled when the agency's finances improved.

"I would be concerned about a significant decline in naturalizations, particularly if qualified applicants are waiting longer to become citizens," Klein said. "Voting is one of the fundamental rights of citizenship, and USCIS itself recognizes the naturalization ceremony as the culmination of that process. USCIS doesn't have to deny citizenship to affect someone's ability to vote. Delaying an otherwise eligible applicant's naturalization until after an election can have the same practical effect."

The second Trump administration has sought to tighten rules around legal immigration, despite President Donald Trump's focus on illegal immigration during his 2024 campaign. Over the past year, numbers of visa approvals and other immigration benefits have fallen at both the State Department, for temporary visitors or new arrivals, and at USCIS, which deals with immigrants within the U.S.

The White House posted to X over the past weekend, celebrating an analysis from The New York Times which outlined these declines, something Melaku said was concerning when USCIS was supposed to be working on approving applications as they come in.

"If they are staffed in these field offices to be adjudicating these processes and not grow the backlog and allow people to have timely and fair adjudications, number one," she said. "Congress does have oversight of this agency, and so then what, in fact, are they prioritizing and why, is one of the questions that we have.

"The second question is, why, if we say we want people to access this process the fair way, and you hear this a lot from the anti-immigrant faction of 'get in line,' these people are in line, they've paid their fees, they're willing to take the oath of citizenship, they've basically submitted their initial paperwork for their green card, they've been vetted. Why are we not making this, in fact, a fair and timely process for these individuals?"

What Does DHS Say?

When asked about the accusation that cases were being deliberately delayed, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek that it was working to undo a policy of "rubber-stamping naturalization applications" under the Biden administration.

"Under the Trump administration, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is reinforcing robust screening and vetting and has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify," a DHS spokesperson said. "This includes reestablishing the 2020 naturalization civics test, strengthening English language proficiency requirements, screening social media for anti-American activities, and ensuring applicants demonstrate good moral character and attachment to the Constitution.

"USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process," the spokesperson said. "Naturalization is a privilege, not a right."

That message has been repeated by Trump's DHS, which has also ramped up denaturalization filings in recent months, with some cases against those who have been American citizens for many years.

Klein, who spent some of his two decades with DHS adjudicating citizenship applications, said the rhetoric around citizenship applications had noticeably shifted since January 2025, including referring to immigrants as "aliens."

"Having personally administered the oath of allegiance, I find that change especially troubling," Klein said. "I remember when the government’s message to new citizens was one of welcome and belonging. Today, I worry that the broader rhetoric sends a very different message, particularly to naturalized Americans who may feel that their citizenship is somehow less secure or less legitimate than that of someone born here.

Klein said that across administrations he worked under, there was a shared understanding that part of USCIS' core mission was to help eligible applicants become Americans, and that when language and priorities shift, the importance of naturalization and the government's commitment to the citizenship it grants was diminished.

"Citizenship is not a political favor granted by an administration. It is a legal right for those who meet the requirements, and USCIS has a responsibility to adjudicate those applications fairly and without unnecessary delay," he said. "When those delays affect whether someone can exercise their right to vote, the consequences extend beyond immigration policy to the integrity of our democracy."

CARLISLE, Iowa (Iowa Capital Dispatch) - A Carlisle couple is suing the federal government over delays in processing the immigration papers for people married to American citizens.

Jordan Sarae Pastrana Bates and her husband, Olman Javie Pastrana Linarez, are suing U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.

The couple, who married in March 2026 and have a child together, alleges that Bates, a U.S. citizen by birth, filed a Petition for Alien Relative, also known as an I-130 application form, with CIS in May 2026 on behalf of her husband, who is a citizen of Honduras.

That application seeks to establish a valid family relationship that would represent the first step in Linarez’s family-based immigration process. Typically, after CIS approves the application, the beneficiary can either apply for an immigrant visa or an adjustment of their residency status.

The lawsuit alleges CIS now takes an average of 80 months, or six and half years, to process I-130 applications, placing the applicants at risk of being deported from the United States.

According to the lawsuit, federal data shows the length of time the federal government takes to process such applications has increased by 420% over the past year, and by 635% in the past five years.

“This is not a marginal delay or a temporary fluctuation,” the couple’s attorney, Jessica Donels, has told the court. “It reflects a systemic failure to process applications in a timely manner.”

The lawsuit seeks a court order that will compel CIS and the other defendants to “perform their duties” as required by law.

The U.S. Department of Justice has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.

Early Wednesday morning, Erik Zepeda was walking to a class at Santa Maria High School when he was detained and injured before being released over a mile from campus by what appeared to him to be Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

20-year-old Zepeda’s former teacher and continuing mentor Glenn Goldin describes Erik with limited verbal communication skills due to disability.

An anonymous spokesperson for ICE stated to The Los Angeles Times that the incident was a case of mistaken identity.

Additionally, the spokesperson says agents responded based on their training to a posture of resistance from Zepeda.

A public affairs officer for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement sent us the following statement:

"On October 21, ICE was conducting a targeted enforcement operation in Santa Maria, California, when they encountered an individual they believed matched the description of the criminal illegal alien target. When the individual resisted officers, refused lawful commands, and assumed a fighting stance with clenched fists, they relied on their training to safely control the situation until they could confirm his identity, whereupon he was released. Claims that the individual suffered broken bones are FALSE [emphasis original]. He never requested medical assistance. ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers. Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training. ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use ‘reasonable suspicion’ to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices. DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence. We know who we are targeting ahead of time. If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability. Our officers are facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats. Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

Zepeda says they handcuffed him and put him in the back of their vehicle to drive around a few city blocks before dropping him off near the place they picked him up.

He says they never asked to see his identification, which he had in his wallet through the whole encounter.

Once released, he finished his walk to school, where an ambulance was called to transport him to the hospital for treatment to his visible injuries.

Local city leaders have expressed their disapproval of the incident, and have demanded an independent investigation.

Santa Maria City Councilwoman Gloria Soto issued a statement on the incident:

"This kind of brutality is not okay. There needs to be an independent investigation into how a case of mistaken identity ended with a student hurt this badly."

As ICE operations escalate across the Central Coast, our most vulnerable community members are being subjected to increasingly aggressive and violent enforcement tactics. This incident raises serious concerns about racial profiling and demands public attention and accountability.

The Santa Maria Police Department says surveillance footage from a grocery store across the street does confirm the incident, and the involvement of federal agents."

The footage and evidence has been turned over to DHS for an investigation.

text:
A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states.

In recent weeks, armed Homeland Security Investigations officers have carried out field operations and visited homes to interview people suspected of illegally voting as noncitizens. The targets can include people who became citizens but voted before they naturalized.

In a 19-page order late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that the federal government was using “flawed” data in the initiative and that its efforts likely violated the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.

Martínez-Olguín referenced a disclosure last month from a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower that alleged rushed efforts to match data to create a target list of potential noncitizens on voter rolls, and that the list includes U.S. citizens. She also pointed to HSI’s social media posts, including one that showed agents handcuffing a California man accused of unlawfully registering to vote.

The judge wrote that the government’s use of unreliable and incomplete data along with highly publicized arrests “lead to an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote.”

HSI field operations were planned in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, according to documents produced in the case and CNN reporting.

Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in those states from conducting field operations targeting people they “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens,” or that are based “wholly” on USCIS matching data without further investigation.

In a declaration, USCIS official Nicolas Bartell had told the judge his team manually reviews records before referring them to HSI, but acknowledged the “low possibility” citizens could be “erroneously identified as potential aliens” in federal records. He wrote the risks were mitigated by safeguards his office takes “and any remaining risks were outweighed by the need to support the agency’s law-enforcement and election-integrity mission.”

It’s unclear how much of an effect the judge’s order will have on the federal government’s highly publicized campaign to find noncitizen voters.

States reviews and audits have consistently found voting by noncitizens to be extremely rare.

“DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders,” the agency wrote in a statement. “We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens.”

The order is set to take effect on Friday and would be in effect through election night, though the federal government could appeal.

The judge’s ruling came in a lawsuit filed last month by a coalition that includes San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, the city of San Francisco, nursing unions and Voto Latino Foundation. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center are litigating the case against the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.

“Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens — whether born here or naturalized — should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them,” Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer with Protect Democracy, said in a statement.

“It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election,” he added.

A court filing by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United described naturalized citizen members who no longer wanted to attend political rallies, sign up to be election poll workers, or vote in person because of the federal operations.

The order comes as the Department of Justice is suing California and demanding the state segregate 20,000 ballots from people federal officials say they believe are “likely” noncitizens.

A preliminary review of a sample of that list by Los Angeles County election officials found many of the registrations were canceled, inactive or had no voting history, and some pertained to people who indicated they were born in the U.S.

The DOJ announced charges against 28 green card holders across the state on Monday who are accused of illegally voting or registering to vote.

WASHINGTON (OSV News) -- A divided D.C. Circuit panel Oct. 20 reversed a lower court ruling and allowed a multifaith coalition to continue its challenge to a Trump administration policy reducing restrictions on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions at what are seen as sensitive locations, including houses of worship.

In 2025, a coalition of more than two dozen religious organizations filed a lawsuit to challenge a Trump administration policy that rescinded long-standing restrictions on arrests at sensitive locations, also including schools and hospitals, with exceptions for public safety or national security threats.

In its ruling, the panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit overturned an April 2025 decision by the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia that the multifaith coalition lacked standing to challenge the Trump administration's rescission of "sensitive locations" protection.

Kelsi Brown Corkran, the Supreme Court director for the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection at Georgetown Law and the lead counsel for plaintiffs, said in a written statement shared with OSV News, "The D.C. Circuit's decision recognizes the real harm that DHS inflicted on religious communities when it rescinded the sensitive locations policy that had protected places of worship from immigration enforcement activity for over three decades."

"It is an important victory for the millions of people of faith represented by the 27 Jewish and Christian denominations and organizations that came together to file this suit in defense of their right to worship and serve their communities without fear of intrusion by ICE officers," Brown Corkran said.

The Rev. Carlos L. Malave, president of Latino Christian National Network, an organization among the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said in a statement, "Our faith calls us to persevere in doing good."

"The Latino Christian National Network celebrates the D.C. Court’s decision regarding our case to protect 'sensitive locations,'" he said. "Houses of worship and sacred spaces must be respected, and the constitutional right of all church members to worship freely and without fear must be safeguarded."

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops was not a plaintiff in the lawsuit but filed an amicus brief in support of the plaintiffs.

That brief argued that the "rescission of the Sensitive Locations Policy at issue here," which the brief noted was in effect for over three decades, "has had the predictable, deleterious effect of forcing Plaintiffs into an untenable position: they either increase the risk to their congregants of harmful enforcement action by maintaining the obligation to attend weekly services, or limit the provision of in-person religious services to their congregants in response to the imminent threat of an enforcement action, and their congregants’ well-founded fears thereof."

They said either scenario presents "severe and concrete" injury that "the courts are ill-suited to dismiss as speculative."

The Trump administration rescinded the long-standing ICE policy -- which prohibits immigration enforcement arrests at certain locations, as well as other sensitive events like weddings and funerals without approval from supervisors -- shortly after he returned to the White House in 2025. The previous policy had exceptions for public safety or national security threats.

In a separate lawsuit, a federal judge previously blocked immigration agents from conducting enforcement operations in houses of worship for Quakers and a handful of other religious groups limited to those who filed that suit.

The city filed suit in U.S. District Court last December to block any attempts of an immigration detention center at its airport. The defendants, which also included the U.S. Coast Guard and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, admitted they planned a detention center at the Newport airport last year and tried unsuccessfully to dismiss the case against them.

The city sought a settlement aimed at keeping a detention center out of the city. But federal officials pushed back deadlines and asked for more time to approve the agreement — much to the annoyance of Newport’s lawyers.

Friday’s settlement lays out that Homeland Security had planned a detention center in Newport and doesn’t necessarily block future plans but only that the agencies must give 30 days notice should it plan a detention center in Newport.

“Under the settlement, ICE has stipulated that it currently has no plans to expand existing detention facilities or open new long- or short-term detention facilities anywhere in Oregon,” the city announced Friday. “The Department of Homeland Security has also agreed to provide the city of Newport with at least 30 days notice before issuing an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement for a plan to construct or operate a detention facility in Newport.”

The legal battle racked up fees with the city’s outside attorneys and several municipalities including Portland, Yachats, Ashland and Benton County have made contributions to its legal funds.

Earlier this month during a status hearing in federal court in Eugene, Stoll Berne attorney Keith Ketterling urged Judge Ann Aiken to set a hard deadline for the government’s final approval. The judge gave Justice Department lawyers until Friday to obtain final approval from their bosses for the negotiated settlement. If the top tier of the federal Justice Department does not sign off on the agreement by then the case would go back into discovery, Aiken said.

On Friday, the agreement was filed, approved and the lawsuit officially dismissed.

“This has been a long and challenging process for our community, and we have remained committed to protecting Newport’s interests every step of the way,” Mayor Jan Kaplan said in a news release Friday.

“Our responsibility is to stand up for our residents, protect our community’s future and ensure that decisions affecting Newport are made with the transparency and accountability our community deserves,” the statement said. “We are pleased to have reached this agreement, and we will continue to keep our community informed.”

text:
Dozens of Boston Dynamics employees are calling on the company to stop the sale of its AI-powered robot dogs to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Known as "Spot," Boston Dynamics' robots are dog-like autonomous machines with four legs that can climb stairs and do backflips. They're equipped with cameras and sensors.

The company faced some backlash in late August, when it was first revealed that the Department of Homeland Security planned to purchase the robots. A $1.3 million contract with ICE was settled in September for the sale of four robot dogs and other Spot technology.

Employees wrote in a petition, obtained by WBUR and sent in early September to company leadership, that the sale hurts Boston Dynamics' image and "presents us as working directly with ICE" as the agency has "worked to sow fear" across the country.

A Boston Dynamics spokesperson confirmed the petition Friday, but said "nearly half" of its 300 signatures were entered as "Anonymous." The company employs more than 1,500 people.

"We cannot be proud of working at [Boston Dynamics] when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians, including some of our own colleagues ... ," the petition read.

ICE previously said the robots would give them an additional safety tool that can "provide real-time situational awareness in hazardous, confined, or tactically uncertain environments" before agents are sent to a scene. The agency had added the robot dogs wouldn't replace "human judgment" from its law enforcement officers.

Boston Dynamics argues the dogs are being sold to ICE's Homeland Security Investigations unit, which primarily focuses on transnational criminal matters — not removal operations.

But Boston Dynamics employees said in the letter that the risk to the company is "too great to continue with this deal," adding it could cause staffers to quit or turn away potential new hires.

"Our public-facing teams have received external emails concerned about this deal," the petition read. "Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is."

In a letter to employees, Boston Dynamics interim CEO Amanda McMaster wrote that after considering the petition, the company is standing by its decision to sell the robots to ICE.

McMaster said customers must comply with the company's terms and conditions for sale, which "prohibit any attempts to weaponize our robot or use it for purposes of harm or intimidation."

"I ask you to respect and accept this decision, even if you do not agree with it," McMaster wrote.

Sherman covered the Supreme Court for the Associated Press for 20 years, and he has previously written about the Justice Department, health care, and national politics.
text:
The Supreme Court already has weighed in on aspects of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, rejecting limits on birthright citizenship, putting the brakes on attempts to deport people using the 18th-century Alien Enemies Act and allowing the administration to revoke protections for immigrants from countries plagued by war, unrest or natural disasters.

Now a new immigration case centered on college campuses is headed the justices’ way. With both the Justice Department and civil rights lawyers representing affected immigrants calling for review and a clear split in appellate rulings, the issue could be ripe for the Court to hear argument and render its judgment by early next summer.

Lawyers for Mahmoud Khalil, arrested in New York City last year because of his activism at Columbia University, and the Trump administration have suggested in court filings that the justices should take up Khalil’s case as well as that of a Georgetown University scholar.

The appeals follow circuit rulings in favor of the government in Khalil’s case and in favor of the Indian scholar, Badar Khan Suri.

“This represents a clear circuit split that will not get resolved absent this Court’s intervention,” Khalil’s lawyers wrote in their petition in Khalil v. Trump, 26-530. The other case is Trump v. Suri, 26-380.

At its root, the dispute concerns the administration’s authority to detain and deport scholars and students over their support for Palestinian rights.

In both cases, Khalil, a legal permanent resident of the U.S. whose wife is an American citizen, and Suri, who holds a visa to do post-doctoral work in this country and also is married to an American, allege they were detained for speaking out in favor of Palestinian rights, in violation of the First Amendment.

Lawyers for Khalil say they have learned that at least a dozen legal permanent residents in the U.S. have been subjected to deportation proceedings based on the same foreign policy ground that Rubio first applied to Khalil.

The issue before the court is somewhat more technical, whether the immigrants can have their constitutional challenges to their detention heard now by federal courts or whether federal law instead directs them first to immigration courts that are part of the Justice Department.

Trump had promised to target students who joined protests against the war in Gaza in 2024. Arrests during the first few months of his second presidential term drew extensive press coverage, perhaps none more than Khalil’s.

He was arrested in March 2025 after Secretary of State Marco Rubio determined that his presence in the United States was contrary to American foreign policy interests, invoking a rarely used broad power to expel foreign students.

At the time, a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security said the arrest was in support of Trump’s “executive orders prohibiting antisemitism” and that Khalil “led activities aligned to Hamas, a designated terrorist organization.”

Less than two weeks later, federal agents detained Suri outside his suburban Washington apartment complex. Suri did not take part in protests, but the administration said he had undisputed family ties to Hamas and wrote social media posts in favor of the group. His wife’s father once served as an adviser to a Hamas leader.

Federal judges eventually ordered the men released. Khalil spent more than three months in detention, mostly in a facility in Louisiana, where he missed the birth of his first child. Suri was held for two months, mainly in Texas.

The Justice Department appealed both rulings in favor of the men, and federal courts of appeals in Philadelphia and Richmond, Virginia, reached different decisions.

A three-judge panel of the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia decided in a 2-1 vote that Khalil’s case belongs in immigration courts, reversing a district court ruling in favor of Khalil.

In an opinion joined by Judges Thomas Hardiman and Stephanos Bibas, the court wrote that the Immigration and Nationality Act stripped federal courts jurisdiction, even as it acknowledged that “some petitioners, like Khalil, will have to wait to seek relief for allegedly unlawful government conduct.”

A three-judge panel of the Fourth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, also voting 2-1, came out the other way. It ruled that Suri’s case was properly in the federal court system, affirming a district court judgment that Suri should be released while the government continues its efforts to deport him.

Describing Suri’s and similar cases, Judge DeAndrea Benjamin wrote that “in each case, the Government insists that judicial review of the allegedly unconstitutional detention can come only after removal proceedings that can last for months or years. Until then, according to the Government, a detained noncitizen has no judicial recourse. We disagree.”

In Khalil’s case, the Justice Department opposed a typically routine request for an extension to file his Supreme Court appeal. Justice Samuel Alito, who oversees matters from the Third Circuit, granted the extension.

Responses in both cases are due in November, and the Supreme Court could consider the petitions shortly before or after its Christmas recess.

Mark Sherman is a regular contributor to Constitution Daily. Sherman covered the Supreme Court for the Associated Press for 20 years, and he has previously written about the Justice Department, health care, and national politics.

title: “Dying in Detention”: Al Jazeera Investigates Immigrant Deaths in California's Adelanto ICE Jail
description:
That’s according to the California attorney general’s report on ICE detention centers in California this year.
The Adelanto ICE Processing Center sits on the edge of the High Desert in California.
NATASHA DEL TORO: As the Trump administration continues to detain record numbers of immigrants, more and more are dying behind bars.
NATASHA DEL TORO: Ismael was born in Mexico and came to the United States undocumented when he was 5.
Also — AMY GOODMAN: Natasha Del Toro — NATASHA DEL TORO: — one more thing I want to mention — AMY GOODMAN: — I want to thank you so much for being with us, and we’re going to link to your documentary, called Dying in Detention.
text:
AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman in Los Angeles. Juan González is in Chicago.

We’re turning now to the rising numbers of deaths in ICE custody. At least 59 people have died in immigration detention since the start of Trump’s second term, the highest in more than a decade, and a growing number of people are dying from medical neglect. Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old legal permanent resident who died earlier this month at an ICE detention center run by the private GEO Group in Laredo, Texas, has complained to his daughter for months about the lack of medical care in detention. At the Adelanto Processing Center, just north of where I am right now in Los Angeles, four out of five recent deaths were linked to substandard medical care. That’s according to the California attorney general’s report on ICE detention centers in California this year.

Journalist Natasha Del Toro and Al Jazeera’s Fault Lines investigated the deaths at the Adelanto Processing Center, which is run, yes, again, by the private GEO Group. This is a clip from the Fault Lines episode Dying in Detention.

JESUS ORTIZ RUIZ: You gotta be literally dying here for you to get sent to the hospital.

NATASHA DEL TORO: We’re traveling to one of the deadliest immigration detention facilities in the United States. The Adelanto ICE Processing Center sits on the edge of the High Desert in California.

JESUS ORTIZ RUIZ: There’s four people in the cell with us. We’re at max capacity right now.

NATASHA DEL TORO: We’ve been speaking with people detained there, people who made it out.

[translated] What are the conditions like inside?

MELVIN: [translated] Not very good.

MELVIN’S DAUGHTER: I’ve never seen him like this.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Is it shocking to see him?

MELVIN’S DAUGHTER: He looks older.

NATASHA DEL TORO: He looks older.

And hearing from family members whose loved one went in and didn’t come out alive.

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: I feel like they’re just treating these people like animals, in a way. None of these deaths should have happened.

NATASHA DEL TORO: As the Trump administration continues to detain record numbers of immigrants, more and more are dying behind bars.

DR. NICHOLAS CUNEO: The number of deaths has more than tripled. The risk of death in ICE detention has never been higher.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Adelanto is run by the for-profit prison company The Geo Group. Four immigrants died there in a recent six-month span. Detainees have fought for better conditions, filing a lawsuit and going on a hunger strike.

JULIUS FREDERICK: They retaliate against you. They just come in, they grab you, and they take you to solitary confinement.

ASHRAF ABUJUMA: They beat me up. I don’t know if you can see, like, bruises all over my body.

AMY GOODMAN: One of the people who died recently at the Adelanto ICE jail in California was Ismael Ayala-Uribe. This is another clip from the documentary Dying in Detention.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Ismael Ayala-Uribe died after becoming sick in an immigration detention center in California in September 2025. He was 39 years old. He was one of more than 50 people to die in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, during President Trump’s first 500 days back in office.

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: He was very protective of, like, not just us, but my mom and dad, too.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Ismael was born in Mexico and came to the United States undocumented when he was 5. He grew up in Southern California and was later granted DACA, a program that gives some immigrants who came here as children temporary protection from deportation.

Was he a good uncle?

JOSE MIGUEL AYALA: He was a good uncle. He was — the kids needed something, he would always go get it, get them school clothes, supplies or whatever they needed, you know? And they do miss him.

NATASHA DEL TORO: He worked at this local car wash just outside Los Angeles for 15 years, supporting his family and eventually becoming the owner’s right-hand man. In 2015, he was convicted of driving under the influence and lost his DACA protections. That left him vulnerable to deportation when President Trump returned to the White House and ramped up immigration raids across the country.

AMY GOODMAN: For more, we’re joined now from Tampa, Florida, by the journalist Natasha Del Toro, investigative correspondent of Fault Lines from Al Jazeera English, the most recent documentary, Dying in Detention.

Watching this documentary, your heart breaks, Natasha. This story of Ismael, 39 years old, dies of an abscess in the year 2026 because an infection that was left to fester goes into his bloodstream. Tell us more about this story.

NATASHA DEL TORO: Yeah, Amy, thank you so much for giving space to this story. It’s so important, and it’s happening right here in our country.

So, as you all noted, Ismael Ayala-Uribe was 39. He came to this country when he was 4 or 5 years old. His parents brought him from Mexico. And he had DACA protections, which he lost because of a DUI. He had lost — he had worked at this car wash for 15 years, was the right-hand man to the owner, and then was picked up in these ICE raids that happened last summer, where they picked up hundreds of workers, people at their place of work, but they figured that — you know, ICE figured that they would be able to get a lot of undocumented people there. And that’s where they picked up Ismael, took him down to Adelanto.

Ismael had gotten sick pretty quickly while he was there. He started complaining of fever. He had chills, started getting very pale. And he was complaining of a sore that was, he said, 10 out of 10 pain. But initially he was ignored when he asked for medical help. Finally, it got so bad that they had to rush him to the infirmary, ended up giving him a Tylenol, which is what we heard over and over again, that they — no matter what they were complaining of, they would get a Tylenol. And they didn’t actually catch the source of the problem, because no one did an examination of the place where he was feeling pain, which was this infected abscess, which, like you said, in 2026, this is really an easy thing to catch. All you need is, you need an antibiotic, is really what you need. But because no one did an examination, no one gave him an antibiotic. He developed sepsis and went into sepsis shock, and ultimately had to go to the emergency room. Finally, they took him to the emergency room. But it’s there that that he died. And we spoke with a physician for human rights who examined — who looked through his medical reports and told us that this was a very preventable death.

Sadly, what we found is that what happened to Ismael is not an isolated incident. This is actually part of a much larger pattern.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And I wanted to ask you, Natasha — he died at 2:30 in the morning, and his family was not notified by ICE. It was the local police that notified them. What is the — how are family able to communicate with those of their family members who are detained in these centers?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Sure. They are able to go to the center. And Lucia, Ismael’s mom, who we spoke to, said she had gone there. Mind you, this is two hours away from Los Angeles. They live in Orange County. And they were driving there as often as they could. So, they were able to communicate with their loved ones by visiting the center. But as you noted, they were not — they were not notified of the death until the next morning, when Lucia and Jose, the brother, got a knock at the door and said that Ismael was dead, that he had passed.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Could I ask you also — the GEO Group announced recently that the Department of Homeland Security had purchased two immigration detention centers in Adelanto for $950 million. What’s the significance of this, of a center going from private ownership to government ownership?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Sure. And this was a very recent announcement that was made. We had actually wrapped up our reporting when we found out that the government had actually purchased the GEO Group. We are not entirely sure why they decided to purchase Adelanto, but what I can tell you is that there are several class-action — there are lawsuits against the Adelanto facility because of the conditions inside. Many of the detainees filed lawsuits. And what we believe is that it becomes harder to sue if it’s in government hands versus if it’s owned by — you know, in private hands. What we do know, though, is that Adelanto is also — it’s going to continue to be run by the GEO Group. So, even though the U.S. government has bought the facility, it’s still going to be operated by GEO.

We also found in our investigation that there were a lot of ties, a lot of conflicts of interest between the federal government and the GEO Group. For example, the director of ICE is somebody who was an executive, a high-level executive, at the GEO Group, somebody named David Venturella. Also, Jim Jordan, who we confront in the film, who is the — you know, he’s the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee. It was leaked that he received, or a PAC tied to him received, a $250,000 contribution from the GEO Group. As a chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, he is supposed to provide oversight of these immigration detention centers, and yet groups tied to him are receiving substantial donations from the GEO Group.

And then, finally, you know, GEO Group has made over a billion dollars in profits from immigration detention. They have given more than a million dollars in campaign — like, to help reelect Donald Trump. So, part of his campaign donations, he received more than a million dollars. So, obviously, that raises a lot of questions for us about these — the relationship between GEO and the federal government and some of these conflicts of interest.

AMY GOODMAN: We just have 30 seconds, Natasha, but I want to ask: Is it possible the number of people who’ve died after medical care failings could be higher, given the rapid deletion of documents by the Trump administration?

NATASHA DEL TORO: Oh, yeah. I mean, we’ve had a hard time giving concrete numbers, mostly because, first, they keep increasing. I mean, someone died just the weekend, a few days ago, in Texas. But also, they recently changed their reporting requirements. So, now ICE does not have to report deaths for anybody held in custody up to 30 days after. They do not have to report those deaths. So, it’s entirely possible that there have been more, that the numbers are not current and they’re not accurate, because they are cutting the requirements, the reporting requirements. Also —

AMY GOODMAN: Natasha Del Toro —

NATASHA DEL TORO: — one more thing I want to mention —

AMY GOODMAN: — I want to thank you so much for being with us, and we’re going to link to your documentary, called Dying in Detention.

title: Oakland Immigration Arrest Raises Questions About 'ICE-Free Zones,' Training at Hospitals
description:
But said, generally, law enforcement does not direct treatment and the system is complying with all laws and requirements concerning immigration enforcement in its facilities.
Ansel Schmidt, a physical therapist at the Highland Hospital, isn’t on the patient’s care team, but helped draft the letter.
Highland Hospital, which sits on county property, also falls under Alameda County’s “ICE-free zone” ordinance that limits cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
County supervisors and advocates touted the policy, of which similar ones have been adopted across the Bay Area, as a way to push back against violent and sometimes deadly actions by immigration agents during the second Trump administration.
In January, agents fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota during a surge of immigration enforcement.
text:
After immigration authorities detained a man in Emeryville last week and brought him to an Alameda County hospital, some medical staff said they didn’t receive legally required training that would have helped them respond to enforcement activity.

Several staff members at Wilma Chan Highland Hospital Campus in Oakland told administrators in a letter that the Oct. 16 arrival of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and a detainee “highlighted major hazards to the rights and safety of our patients.”

Immigration agents brought a man to Highland for treatment after an agent allegedly tackled him and fractured six of his ribs, said Nikolas De Bremaeker, an attorney at Centro Legal De La Raza who represents the man.

Since then, De Bremaeker and some employees said agents allegedly tried to obstruct access to counsel, to direct medical treatment and to ask staff for medical information. The agent who tackled the patient, the attorney said, has been “sitting on his bed, grinning at him.”

“It’s incredibly scary,” De Bremaeker told KQED. “It’s just unacceptable for ICE agents to be terrorizing folks inside a hospital.”

About two dozen community members were on the lookout for agents on Thursday morning for hours, being directed by others to make noise if immigration authorities exited or entered the facility. They’d been showing up since Monday, an organizer said.

The Alameda Health System, which Highland is a part of, declined to comment on allegations specific to De Bremaeker’s client’s care, citing patient confidentiality. But said, generally, law enforcement does not direct treatment and the system is complying with all laws and requirements concerning immigration enforcement in its facilities.

In an earlier statement to KQED about the ICE activity, AHS said that it activated an Incident Command Center and that security personnel are on site monitoring developments.

“We are following all immigration response protocols,” AHS said in the statement.

Some staff members told AHS in the letter that they “at all levels, remain confused and consistently express a lack of clarity on policy when patients are brought in civil detention.”

“This is out of step with current best practices in the state of California,” the staff members wrote.

Senate Bill 81, which took effect in September 2025, requires medical health care providers to restrict certain immigration information from being shared and, as part of new restrictions to nonpublic areas, facilities must inform staff on how to respond to requests to access sites and establish procedures for receiving visitors.

But staff told administrators the hospital system isn’t in compliance with that law.

Ansel Schmidt, a physical therapist at the Highland Hospital, isn’t on the patient’s care team, but helped draft the letter.

“I’m not sure that I’ve received anything that I would call training,” Schmidt told KQED. What Schmidt has received is a “badge buddy,” or a reference guide, that he said implies staff can cooperate with ICE.

A badge buddy reviewed by KQED shows that staff are instructed to notify an administrator when a patient in ICE custody shows up for care. Providers request agents leave during evaluation, inform patients of their rights and, if they don’t meet admission criteria, can be handed off to the ICE control office.

Iman Khalil, a respiratory therapist at San Leandro Hospital, part of the Alameda Health System, said staff members receive minimal training about what to do when immigration authorities show up. Khalil received the same badge and emails Schmidt did.

“Allowing the agents in the hospital … undoes all that training,” Khalil said. “You really don’t think they’ll even allow the agents in the hospital. But here we are.”

AHS CEO James Jackson told staff that AHS believed the man in ICE’s custody at the hospital was part of the agency’s civil immigration enforcement authority and called on personnel to review established immigration response protocols, according to an Oct. 19 email obtained and reviewed by KQED.

Highland Hospital, which sits on county property, also falls under Alameda County’s “ICE-free zone” ordinance that limits cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

County supervisors and advocates touted the policy, of which similar ones have been adopted across the Bay Area, as a way to push back against violent and sometimes deadly actions by immigration agents during the second Trump administration. In January, agents fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota during a surge of immigration enforcement.

But Alameda County Sheriff Yesenia Sanchez and other officials have also noted the limits of just how far the ICE-free zone can go. It doesn’t prevent immigration officials from actually being on county property, Sanchez said previously. Officials in other jurisdictions with these “zones” have even referred to them as symbolic — or a way to create “false expectations.”

De Bremaeker said his client is still in ICE custody as of Thursday afternoon. Another man he represents was detained by ICE in the San Antonio neighborhood in Oakland on the same day, before being taken to another hospital for injuries that De Bremaeker said were sustained because of the officers’ actions.

The two cases are part of an “unprecedented escalation” of violence from ICE, De Bremaeker said.

The attorney called on federal lawmakers to launch a congressional inquiry into ICE’s actions and, in particular, the agency’s activity in hospitals.

“They have been occupying these hospitals for days, creating an incredible threat to community members, terrifying folks who need medical care from going to the hospital,” De Bremaeker said.

Renee Coe, with the Party for Socialism and Liberation, is among the community members who came out to keep watch for ICE at the hospital. She said some community members are scared to show up to the hospital because of federal agents’ presence, but urged them not to put off medical care.

AHS said its property is not being used as a staging area, operations base or processing location for immigration enforcement activities, and the immigration vehicles currently on Highland property are present “only in connection with a patient who is in immigration enforcement custody.”

Several Oakland residents are holding an emergency press conference at 6 p.m. on Friday in front of Highland to demand the release of De Bremaeker’s client and accountability for local authorities, security contracting with the facility and AHS “continuously” assisting ICE operations at the hospital.

We will continue fighting to ensure that no one, not even this administration, is above the Constitution.”
text:
Oct 23 Friday, Washington DC — In response to today’s U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruling in Sosnava Rodriguez v. Ortega, a case concerning noncitizens’ constitutional right to challenge their detention when they are held without access to a bond hearing, the American Immigration Council and the National Immigration Project issued the following statements:

“Today’s ruling is an affront to the U.S. Constitution. The principle at stake here is simple: if the government wants to detain someone, it has to explain why depriving them of their liberty is necessary. And anyone who is detained has the right to ask a judge for review of that detention. Instead, this ruling allows the government to lock people up when detention plainly serves no purpose, and without any way to challenge it,” said Rebecca Cassler, senior litigation attorney at the American Immigration Council, who argued the case before the Fifth Circuit. “The right to due process is a fundamental constitutional protection, and it is meant to protect every person in this country. Because of today’s decision, that right is hollow for immigrants in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi. But the logic of the Fifth Circuit’s decision threatens everyone in this country: when courts degrade the meaning of liberty for some, we all suffer the consequences. We will continue fighting to ensure that no one, not even this administration, is above the Constitution.”

text:
President Donald Trump said he told his administration to file a lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, kicking off what many fear could become a lengthy battle between the government and states over certifying an election where the president's party is struggling.

"I'm the one that said do it," Trump told reporters as he landed for a campaign rally in Florida.

The lawsuit centers on one of the president's longstanding complaints in the Senate race — the presence of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who Republicans fear could siphon away votes from the incumbent in what's likely to be a photo-finish contest with Democrat Mary Peltola, the state's former congresswoman.

The second Dan Sullivan, who is Daniel J. Sullivan from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg, has said he decided to run on his own, but Republicans have contended he is a Democratic plant to siphon votes away from their candidate.

The lawsuit Thursday by the Republican president's Department of Justice in federal court in Alaska demands that the state be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. Sullivan remains on the ballot. "The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska," the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.

The legal challenge came 11 days before the Nov. 3 election and months after the final ballot was set.

The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, and the state's Republican officials made the decisions about how to list him on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent. Alaska's ranked choice voting system also will allow voters to select both of the men if confused.

Peltola and Sen. Sullivan were top vote-getters in nonpartisan primary

The senator received more than 68,000 votes in the August primary, while the challenging Sullivan got 4,107, about 2% of the total vote. Peltola, who had previously served one term in the House, was the top vote-getter in the nonpartisan primary. Both parties expect that whoever wins in November will do so by a tight margin in a state of 738,000 people.

The campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan did not address whether the senator supports the Department of Justice's intervention. "We'll let the DOJ complaint run its course," campaign spokesman Nate Adams said in a text message. "Alaskans can tell the difference between a Democrat sideshow and Senator Sullivan's strong record of delivering for Alaska."

Daniel J. Sullivan, whose presence on the ballot is at issue in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Donald Trump knows that Dan Sullivan is going to lose the election, so now his Department of Justice is filing a sham lawsuit to overturn the will of Alaska voters and steal an election when he loses," said Devan Barber, executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Watch the segment in the player above.

In a statement on Friday, the Department of Justice noted that Alaska's election officials, who are Republicans, determined the other Sullivan's campaign was an attempt to "mislead:" voters and wanted him removed from the ballot. Both a state court and Alaska's Supreme Court disagreed and kept the second Sullivan on the ballot.

"The Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska's election or the will of its voters," the DoJ statement said.

The Department of Justice has increasingly been used to bolster the president's political operation, targeting his enemies and suing Democratic-controlled states before the election. Democrats and many voting rights advocates have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that Trump's party loses, much as he unsuccessfully tried to do when he lost the White House race to Democrat Joe Biden.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. "It is not DOJ's intention to, and it's never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process," he told reporters Thursday in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.

The lawsuit was signed by Associate U.S. Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who represented Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants before becoming one of the top appointees at the department.

Constitution gives states the power to run elections

Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race and that it probably would not survive long. "The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Muller said. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."

The U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards set by Congress. That division of power has frustrated Trump, who repeatedly has tried to seize control of election procedures through executive orders that courts have blocked.

READ MORE: How the phrase 'Lower 48' became a fixture in Alaska's high-stakes Senate race

The final step for a state election is formally certifying the winner, the act that the administration's lawsuit seeks to prevent, it requests, "pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for. Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."

The process in Alaska is complicated by the state's ranked choice voting system, which Trump opposes, and many expect it to take weeks before a winner is known. Also on the state's ballot is an initiative to repeal that system.

Trump has stepped up complaints about a ballot with dueling Sullivans

Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan's presence on the ballot, making reference to it during a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week where he called it "CHEATING."

"We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness," the president wrote on Wednesday.

Clogging a ballot with third party candidates to siphon off votes from the other major party is a long-standing tactic in the country's two-party system. Republicans have been linked to an effort to persuade Ohio voters to support a socialist in that state's Senate race, which could help Republican Sen. Jon Husted fend off a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington, D.C. contributed to this report.

Amid a “bizarre” federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar’s citizenship, President Donald Trump called on the Minnesota Democrat to “IMMEDIATELY resign” from her seat, accusing her of using a fake name.

“Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, her real name, has openly admitted to FRAUD, and she will not be legally allowed to be a Member of this August Body from this point forth,” Trump continued.

Trump’s post on Oct. 22 came amid a probe from the Trump administration aimed at revoking Omar’s American citizenship and deporting her, if investigators can prove that she or her relatives lied to immigration authorities when she became a citizen, according to previous USA TODAY reporting.

In an appearance on Fox News on Oct. 22, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington, DC, reiterated the president’s point, saying Omar’s name could be part of the ongoing probe.

“So the question is, who is Ilhan Omar, and has she followed all of the laws as it relates to naturalization and immigration,” Pirro said.

A scare tactic

In an appearance on MSNOW this week, Omar said the probe, which included a predawn search of her Washington, DC, home, was part of a scare tactic by the Trump administration.

"You don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out," she said.

The raid at her home began at 6 a.m., she said, describing how she had been asleep for barely two and a half hours when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents pounded on the front and back doors. She said she thought something was on fire.

When they left, Omar said, they carried 17 items, among them her youngest daughter’s first phone, a camera her husband’s uncle had kept from his years in the Navy, and a book her husband had been using to learn Somali.

USA TODAY’s María Luisa Paúl and Zachary Schermele contributed to this report.

text:
A federal appeals court on Friday stripped due process rights from hundreds of immigrants held by Immigration and Custom Enforcement.

In a 10–7 en banc decision, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that ICE detainees with pending immigration hearings are not entitled to receive a bond hearing, where a judge could assess their dangerousness and flight risk, regardless of how long they have been in detention.

The decision blocks efforts by federal judges who have been ordering the release of hundreds of immigrants—many of whom have no criminal record and have deep ties to the United States—held without bond by ICE’s mass deportation policy.

After the Fifth Circuit upheld ICE’s policy in February, other federal judges discovered that they were able to argue that detention violated immigrants’ constitutional due process rights. In the past year, judges have ruled against detentions without bond more than 21,150 times. The Fifth Circuit has now choked off that legal argument.

The case will likely head to the Supreme Court, which is set to decide on a number of immigration reform cases in the coming term.

The Justice Department charged two former FBI agents Friday with lying to Congress during the Hunter Biden laptop investigation.

Former intelligence analyst Nikki Floris, who ran the intelligence division at the Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, a former deputy assistant director for counterintelligence, surrendered on arrest warrants earlier Friday. During the following hearing in Washington, U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui said that the case pertained to “Hunter Biden’s laptop, investigations around that.”

Floris’s attorney condemned the charges in a statement. “Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the [Justice Department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” the statement said. The charges come just 10 days before the midterms.

The laptop scandal began in December 2019, when a Wilmington, Delaware–area computer repair shop owner gave an abandoned laptop purportedly belonging to Biden to Donald Trump’s former personal attorney Rudy Giuliani. Giuliani then handed a copy of the laptop’s hard drive to local law enforcement, which handed over the contents to the FBI.

In the years that followed, Republicans leveraged the laptop’s myriad contents to escalate scrutiny and speculation surrounding the Biden family’s business dealings with Burisma, a Ukrainian natural gas and energy company.

Giuliani and Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist, insisted that the laptop contained evidence that the Biden family made millions of dollars after former President Joe Biden and a Burisma adviser held a meeting. (The New York Post, which ran the original story on its front page, later said that the contents of the laptop were mixed with fake material and that most of the data could not be verified.)

The alleged meeting became central to an impeachment probe against the elder Biden. Republicans claimed at the time that Biden had engaged in corruption, and had peddled the influence of his vice presidency to rake in cash.

Floris and Benavides briefed Republican lawmakers in 2020 about the contents of the laptop as part of a congressional investigation. Senator Chuck Grassley has since claimed that the pair gave the briefing in order to cast the probe as Russian disinformation.

But the entire investigation fell apart in 2024 after its star witness, Alexander Smirnov, admitted the conspiracy was in fact Russian disinformation. Smirnov admitted to Justice Department prosecutors that “officials associated with Russian intelligence were involved” in fabricating the Hunter Biden narrative. In the ensuing fallout, Smirnov told investigators he was in contact with “four different [top] Russian officials,” two of whom were the “heads of the entities they represent.”

President Trump brushed aside questions Friday about interruptions to Starlink service for Ukraine, following complaints from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy earlier in the day.

“You must know now who ordered the Starlink access in Ukraine to be restricted. Who was it?” a reporter asked Trump outside of the White House. Trump denied any knowledge, and replied, “Well, I wouldn’t tell you if I did,” asking who the reporter worked for. When she said, “CNN,” he chuckled.

“Why would I tell CNN?” Trump said, before saying the network did some “nice polls” on him recently.

Earlier in the day, Zelenskiy said regarding Starlink that “the speed has not been restored,” despite Trump’s claim that Elon Musk, who owns the company, had restored access. Ukrainian military and government officials told The Wall Street Journal that connections were failing at higher drone speeds, hurting defense capabilities. Another reporter asked Trump if he had told Musk to stop messing around with Ukraine’s connection.

“I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” Trump said.

Trump and Musk are each blaming each other for the decision to throttle Ukraine’s Starlink service last week, which allowed Russia to launch a massive aerial attack on the country. The Wall Street Journal earlier this week reported that Musk in fact ordered internet speeds to slow down, and discussed the decision with Trump ahead of time.

The White House was involved in the FBI’s Epstein files cover-up all along.

The FBI’s July 2025 Epstein files memo immediately blew up in the bureau’s face. Its declaration that there was no “client list,” no punishable co-conspirators, and no grounds for further investigation both infuriated the president’s MAGA voter base and started the long domino effect that would eventually oust ex–Attorney General Pam Bondi.

Trump administration messages obtained by Raw Story revealed Friday that Taylor Budowich, then the White House deputy chief of staff, had his fingers in the FBI’s drafting process prior to the memo’s public release.

“Have something I can edit?” Budowich emailed FBI Director Kash Patel two weeks before the memo was released. The email’s subject line read: “Re: Draft memo from DOJ—we have not edited it yet.”

“Just got it from DOJ. Here you go. Thanks,” Patel responded hours later.

The next day, Budowich told Patel that he had passed the draft along to the White House communications team, noting that the message needed to be pasted on DOJ and FBI letterhead, according to Raw Story.

Almost a week later, then–Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche sent a “final version” to Budowich. It failed to meet Budowich’s expectations, however, lacking the identifying seal of the Justice Department.

“I need a version on letterhead,” Budowich repeated. “Someone needs to own this. I can’t give a doc to a reporter that could easily be confused with a [high school] term paper, so need to provide some validation of the doc.”

Diego Pestana, Blanche’s counsel, fulfilled Budowich’s request an hour and a half later.

“These records show that Kash Patel worked hand in hand with the former White House deputy chief of staff on the 2025 DOJ-FBI memo, which stated there would be no further investigation or release of the Epstein files,” Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics and anti-corruption at the Democracy Defenders Fund, told Raw Story.

“It’s deeply concerning that the FBI coordinated with the White House on this memo, given President Trump’s well-documented association with Jeffrey Epstein and Trump’s frequent mention in the files,” Swartz added.

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit to block Alaska from certifying its Senate election results in the event that Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. This move is the Trump administration’s most blatant effort to swing ballots in Republicans’ favor this November.

The lawsuit alleges that the Senate election should be nullified if Sullivan loses because there’s another “Daniel J. Sullivan” on the ballot also running as a Republican, and the Trump administration thinks voters will be too confused—even though Dan Sullivan is properly listed as the incumbent on the ballot.

“Daniel J. Sullivan decided to run for Senator in 2026 as a Republican with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him,” the DOJ lawsuit alleges. “The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.”

The lawsuit raised alarm across the political sphere.

“Surprising that the president who tried to end American democracy and stay in power even though he lost is queuing up additional ways to try to end democracy in America,” the Center for American Progress’s Bobby Kogan mused online.

“Election Day isn’t the end of the fight,” the Lincoln Project’s Rick Wilson wrote. “Get ready to get loud.”

“Trump isn’t going to try to interfere in the midterms, he’s already getting started,” chimed journalist Pedro L. Gonzalez. “They’re going to do this everywhere they think they can get away with it.”

This lawsuit comes just a day after Attorney General and former Trump personal attorney Todd Blanche admitted that he was open to blocking states from certifying elections. Now his DOJ is attempting to do just that.
