description:
The Fresno City Council voted Thursday to set up a $1 million legal defense fund to support immigrants in the city facing threats of deportation.
The legal aid comes amid a surge in immigration enforcement across California and the Central Valley in the lead up to the midterm elections.
Immigrant rights groups and advocates applauded the move on Thursday with 17 total speakers urging the council to approve it.
This isn’t the first time the city has allocated funds toward legal defense for immigrants.
The council previously allocated $200,000 toward a legal defense fund five years ago in another split vote.
text:
What’s at stake?

The council approved allocating a record amount of funds toward legal aid for immigrants in the city facing threats of deportation on Thursday, as well as a new designated zone for vendors in the Tower District on weekends after a string of violent incidents on Olive Avenue.

The Fresno City Council voted Thursday to set up a $1 million legal defense fund to support immigrants in the city facing threats of deportation.

The agenda item, sponsored by Councilmember Miguel Arias, passed with an amendment restricting eligibility to residents of the city who have not been convicted of any criminal offense.

The legal aid comes amid a surge in immigration enforcement across California and the Central Valley in the lead up to the midterm elections.

Immigrant rights groups and advocates applauded the move on Thursday with 17 total speakers urging the council to approve it.

“There is no right to a court-appointed attorney in immigration court. That means when a Fresno resident is detained, they can be facing deportation in just a couple days with no one in their corner,” said Sukaina Hussain, the deputy executive director of the California Immigrant Policy Center.

“Having a lawyer and having a fund that can provide support for this attorney can severely change that outcome,” she continued, “and can help keep families together.”

Hussain added in her comments that she hopes the investment isn’t just a one-time thing and that she hopes the city partners with “trusted” service providers in the community to offer the legal aid.

Two members of the public spoke out against the fund, including Neil O’Brien, who said that by creating a special legal benefit for one group of residents, the fund “creates two classes of people.”

Councilmembers approved the establishment of the fund 5-1 in a sweeping vote on the council’s consent agenda for the day with Councilmember Nick Richardson registering the lone “no” vote. Council Vice President Tyler Maxwell was absent from Thursday’s meeting.

Richardson originally pulled the item from the consent agenda for discussion, although Councilmember Mike Karbassi successfully motioned to move it back onto consent with the amendment restricting eligibility added on.

This isn’t the first time the city has allocated funds toward legal defense for immigrants. The council previously allocated $200,000 toward a legal defense fund five years ago in another split vote.

Karbassi voted against the budget motion in 2021 that created the fund, alongside a slew of other budget motions. He said in an email to Fresnoland on Tuesday that his vote in 2021 was as a result of promising voters he would vote against any budget that failed to add additional police officers and firefighters to the force, and that it had nothing to do with the individual budget motion itself.

New rules for vendors in the Tower District take effect Thursday

Following a tense, three-hour community meeting the night before, the council voted on Thursday to enact the last of several sweeping changes they say are aimed at enhancing safety in the Tower District neighborhood.

In their vote Thursday, the council greenlit the creation of a designated zone for vendors in the Tower District on weekends, located in the vacant lot on the southwest corner of Olive and Van Ness Avenues.

For the next 90 days, vendors in Tower will be restricted to that lot “between the hours of 6:00 p.m. Thursday to 6 a.m. Monday,” city documents say.

“We’re going to test this out for 90 days, see what works, see what doesn’t work, and hopefully continue to adjust as needed,” said Councilmember Annalisa Perea, who represents the Tower District north of Olive.

“We want to make sure that the vendors are safe as well,” said Mayor Jerry Dyer, “and so we’ve already put in increased lighting on the property, as well as (a) security camera, and we’ll have police presence on that corner as well.”

The council approved the pilot program 6-0 with only brief remarks from the dais and virtually no public comment either in support of or opposition to the new rules.

In an interview following Thursday’s meeting, Veva Islas, a longtime advocate for the city’s mobile food vendors, called the pilot a “positive step forward.”

“I had asked the city to do this a long time ago,” she said. “I have been a proponent (of) establishing designated areas for vendors where they can operate without worry about being booted or unwelcome there.

“I think that’s a positive step forward, especially in contrast to the last ordinance that was really trying to dissuade vendors from being in the Tower,” she added, “and really blaming vendors for the problems of the Tower.”

Islas also had some notes on how the city should ideally implement the program, which is set to go into effect immediately on Thursday night.

“I would say at the front of the line to have space in this lot should be vendors who have their food-handling certification, vendors who have their license with the city, vendors who have their permit with environmental health and vendors who are improving the food environment: that (are) making healthy options available to community members,” she said.

Some vendors, including Crystal Sandoval, operator of Casa del Sazon food truck, have several lingering questions about how the new lot will be run.

“Is it going to be first come, first serve every single time?” she said in an interview Thursday following the meeting. “Or are we going to be taking turns if other vendors want to sell?

“Can we park at that spot during the week as well, or is it only from Thursday and on?”

City council moves forward with pursuing new restrictions for sex offender housing

The council passed several other items on the consent agenda on Thursday, including approving a two-year agreement for the Advance Peace program amounting to $950,000 and a $4.3 million contribution toward an affordable, modular housing project for seniors along the Blackstone corridor to be built by Samuelian Group LLC.

Councilmembers also approved a resolution, sponsored by Karbassi, to explore the feasibility of introducing an ordinance to restrict the number of group homes for sex offenders in the city.

Fresno County passed similar legislation this year, although they were slapped with a lawsuit soon after in February, brought by the Alliance for Constitutional Sex Offense Laws.

Richardson sided with the rest of the council in voting to approve the resolution but said he was skeptical whether the proposed ordinance would hold up against legal scrutiny.

He also pointed to a similar proposal brought forward by Councilmember Diane Pearce in Clovis, “specifically by someone else who happens to be running for office right now,” Richardson added.

Karbassi is in the middle of a campaign for the District 1 seat on the Fresno County Board of Supervisors, while Pearce has said she’ll run for Supervisor Nathan Magsig’s seat if he wins in his bid for the state legislature this November.

“I think getting sued, when it comes to a violent sexual predator, is worth the risk,” Karbassi said in response to Richardson’s concerns.

text:
In 2006, a law professor coined the term “crimmigration,” defining the convergence of immigration and criminal law as the most important immigration law development to date.

Twenty years later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement crackdown on immigrants in the country without legal permission is drawing even more attention to the legal specialty and what the term means now.

“We’re seeing a rise in detention cases. And that detention brings the crimmigration issues to the forefront,” said Kevin Muñoz, founding attorney at Muñoz Legal, a criminal defense and immigration law firm in Indianapolis.

In the past, criminal convictions such as aggravated felonies, crimes involving moral turpitude and controlled substance offenses typically triggered immigration repercussions. However, Indiana attorneys are now witnessing minor offenses leading to immigration issues.

“Driving without a license rarely put us in front of an immigration judge. It does now,” said Paraskevi “Patty” Xidias, an Indianapolis immigration attorney. “Many things that wouldn’t have pulled somebody into an immigration proceeding are now bringing them in.”

In a new evolution of crimmigration, Hoosier criminal defense and immigration lawyers are taking on more work, navigating the complexities of both fields, and reaching out to each other to act in the best interests of their clients.

“We are seeing in the removal defense world a huge increase in the detention and removal of non-criminal immigrants,” said Sarah L. Burrow, an immigration attorney at Lewis Kappes. “However, we are seeing those who do have some sort of criminal history being detained at higher rates than before.”

About crimmigration

Lewis & Clark Law School Professor Juliet Stumpf saw the crimmigration merger taking place on three fronts.

She noted in a 2006 American University Law Review article that the substance of immigration law and criminal law increasingly overlap, immigration enforcement has come to resemble criminal law enforcement, and the procedural aspects of prosecuting immigration violations have taken on many earmarks of the criminal side.

But because “the convergence of immigration and criminal law” broadly describes crimmigration, Xidias notes a clear definition of the legal practice can be hard to pin down.

“Most of us interpret it to mean anytime that there’s any type of criminal issues related to our immigration cases, which can include simply entering the country without permission,” she said. “But it could be DUIs, leaving the scene of an accident. Those are the typical types of cases we see. But they can include more serious crimes like fraud and murder.”

Burrow sees her role in crimmigration as navigating immigration laws for people with criminal charges or convictions.

“[Crimmigration] is the immigration consequences of criminal activity,” she said. “We only practice immigration [law]. But we’re well-versed in crimmigration because we do a lot of removal defense.”

As a firm that specializes in both criminal defense and immigration law, Muñoz Legal is equipped to help people placed into immigration custody and removal proceedings through criminal charges, preventing clients from having to seek additional counsel.

“When people come to us, we can let them know, ‘Hey, we have attorneys who can focus on your criminal case, and then we have attorneys who can focus on your immigration case. It’s an advantage just because of how intertwined it is,” Muñoz said.

What’s changed

While driving without a license and other minor crimes like shoplifting can now lead to immigration problems, Burrow says a noncitizen’s confession to law enforcement also can cause issues.

“Sometimes even admitting to the essential elements of a crime, let’s say, during an arrest, even that can be enough to impact an immigration case, even if there’s no conviction ultimately,” she said.

Burrow acknowledged more green card holders are being detained at airports after returning from international trips because of decades-old criminal records that never mattered before.

“It may not even be something that ultimately renders them inadmissible or removable, but because it exists at all, it’s being flagged, and they’re being put into detention,” Burrow said. “[President Donald Trump’s administration is] casting such a wide net that everyone’s getting caught in it.”

“We are advising against any travel right now, even to our green card holders,” added Xidias. “If they don’t have to go, we’re advising them not to go.”

The lawyers describe the difficulty of securing bonds for noncitizens, even in minor cases such as driving without a license. Muñoz says more judges are classifying this type of misdemeanor offender as a danger to the community.

“We’re also seeing more aggressive immigration detention where they’re not receiving due process. They’re not able to speak to a lawyer,” Muñoz said. “A lot of times, immigration will prioritize removal over most criminal cases. So, they’re not releasing them from custody to be able to even defend themselves against charges.”

An attorney’s duty

With an uptick in detention cases raising awareness about the intricacies of crimmigration, the first step for criminal defense lawyers is to ask each client about citizenship status. That best practice was noted by the Indiana Supreme Court in the majority opinion in Bobadilla v. State, 117 N.E.3d 1272 (2019).

This appellate ruling held “that counsel rendered ineffective assistance” by failing to properly advise Bobadilla about the immigration consequences of a misdemeanor guilty plea. In the original case, the attorney marked “N/A” next to the advisement form paragraph about citizenship and immigration status without asking the defendant, who was a non-citizen.

“That’s a perfect picture of crimmigration in Indiana because it’s the culmination of a lot of different moving parts,” said Muñoz, who represented Bobadilla during post-conviction relief proceedings. “Ineffective assistance of counsel is a crux of the post-conviction issue in the crimmigration world.”

While Burrow urges non-citizens with criminal cases to consult immigration counsel to learn how outcomes could affect their status, a precedent set by the U.S. Supreme Court in Padilla v. Kentucky, 559 U.S. 356 (2010) states that “defense attorneys must inform non-citizen criminal defendants about the risk of deportation based on a conviction when they are deciding whether to plead guilty.”

“Just to make sure, taking this plea agreement, or if you go to trial, and you’re convicted, what could happen? For a long time, [criminal defense lawyers] weren’t doing that,” said Jordan Paicely, associate attorney at Muñoz Legal.

For example, under federal immigration law, a state-classified misdemeanor carrying a 365-day sentence can be treated as an aggravated felony, which is a deportable offense.

“When you have these crimes, like a theft or what would be considered a crime of violence, literally one day can make a difference,” Paicely said. “If it’s one year, it makes you ineligible for so much relief in immigration. If the defense attorney knew about this, they could help in that negotiation with the prosecutors saying, ‘Hey, can you just take it down one day to save this guy, give him a chance?’”

Working together

Muñoz mentioned that several criminal defense lawyers have called his office asking for advice on immigration issues. The firm has also spoken to the Marion County Public Defender Agency about spotting problems that may arise when criminal defense and immigration law cross paths.

By working longer hours and more days per week, Burrow’s team has become more cohesive since the immigration case influx. The demand has prompted the firm to explore federal practice.

“It would have been unusual in the past for us to file anything in the district court, but now we’re finding that we have to bypass the immigration courts and go straight to the district court for relief, whether that’s through habeas [corpus] or mandamus,” Burrow said. “We’re expanding our practice to accommodate those needs and getting good at something we didn’t regularly do.

“It requires a lot of creative lawyering and for us to stay on top of all the changes.”

Although Xidias refers criminal bond cases to immigration attorneys with stronger criminal defense backgrounds, she uses resources such as the local American Immigration Lawyers Association network to deal with other case challenges.

“We rely on each other a lot because we can’t handle all the workload at this point,” Xidias said. “We share who is able to handle different types of relief and communicate with each other on what we’re seeing and the trends and how we’ve each been able to successfully approach things and what hasn’t worked.”•

At the same time, Catron remains to this day a somewhat “obscure figure,” with not one full-length biography to his name.
In 1824, the Tennessee Legislature elected Catron to the state’s Supreme Court of Errors and Appeals, then Tennessee’s highest court, where he served for seven years.
As chief justice, Catron upheld the freeing of a group of enslaved people in an 1834 case, but only on the condition that they leave the United States.
Catron dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not blockade Southern ports without Congress’ approval.
text:
Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John Catron, who served on the court from 1837 to 1865.

Justice John Catron was a man of contradictions – for example, a southern slaveholder, he also opposed the secession of Tennessee while on the court and sought to preserve the Union. At the same time, Catron remains to this day a somewhat “obscure figure,” with not one full-length biography to his name.

Catron’s birthplace and date are uncertain, with some sources putting it in Pennsylvania around 1786, and others in Virginia between 1781 and 1792. What is known is that he was born into a poor German family, had minimal schooling, married in 1807, and, by 1812, settled in Sparta, Tennessee. Not long after, Catron served as a private under then-General Andrew Jackson in the Alabama campaigns against the Creek Indians and the War of 1812, reportedly becoming so ill that he had to be brought back to Tennessee in a wagon. (Some sources say he also fought in the Battle of New Orleans.)

Catron was licensed to practice law in 1815 and then served as a prosecutor on a Tennessee “mountain circuit.” He relocated to Nashville in 1818, and soon had a thriving practice centered on land law and disputes. In 1824, the Tennessee Legislature elected Catron to the state’s Supreme Court of Errors and Appeals, then Tennessee’s highest court, where he served for seven years. His best-known ruling there was reportedly one in 1829 that disbarred a lawyer for fighting a duel in Kentucky. Catron rejected the argument that a duel amounted to an “honorable homicide” and wrote that the law treated it as “a wicked and wilful [sic] murder.” In 1831, he became the court’s first chief justice and served for three more years. As chief justice, Catron upheld the freeing of a group of enslaved people in an 1834 case, but only on the condition that they leave the United States. The next year, he upheld Tennessee’s extension of its criminal laws over Cherokee land inside the state.

Catron’s involvement in politics reportedly led to his chief justiceship ending; one scholar writes that then-presidential-candidate Hugh Lawson White’s allies forced Catron off the bench after he backed Martin Van Buren over White in the 1836 election, while another account says the legislature retaliated for his backing of Van Buren by abolishing the Court of Errors and Appeals altogether. Catron then went on to manage Van Buren’s Tennessee campaign.

Catron’s support for Van Buren and “align[ment] with Jacksonian democracy” led to Jackson nominating Catron to the Supreme Court on his last full day as president on March 3, 1837, the same day that Congress added two seats to the Supreme Court (bringing it to nine). Five days after Jackson’s nomination, with Van Buren now in the White House, the Senate confirmed Catron by a vote of 28 to 15.

Catron “never sought to take a leading part in the great public questions before the Supreme Court,” instead opting for opining on “complex technical matters” and the common law. Averaging 7.5 opinions per term (a lower rate than any Taney Court colleague except Justice James Wayne), Catron usually sided with Chief Justice Roger Taney and often took cases over Spanish land grant disputes. Catron did make clear some of his own views; in the 1853 case of Ohio Life Insurance & Trust Co. v. Debolt, he warned against the rapid growth of corporations, writing that “these numerous bodies of associated wealth” risked “stand[ing] above the state government creating them.”

Catron’s most significant moment on the court came in the 1857 case of Dred Scott v. Sandford, where he agreed in his concurrence that Congress lacked the power to prevent slavery in the western territories and that Scott remained enslaved. While the case was pending, he also wrote privately to then-president-elect James Buchanan, asking him to persuade Justice Robert Grier to join the majority (Grier ultimately did so).

Catron enslaved people throughout his life, and in 1827 he reportedly fathered a son whom he never acknowledged with Sally, an enslaved woman. However, Catron did not follow Tennessee out of the Union and in 1861 returned to Nashville to try to persuade the state’s leaders not to secede. After they declined, he left for Kentucky and his property in Tennessee was confiscated. He kept riding circuit in Kentucky and Missouri, and when the army locked up civilians who sympathized with the Confederacy, Catron turned away their requests for habeas corpus, effectively supporting the detentions. Once federal forces took control of Nashville, he went back and opened the U.S. district court there in June 1862. Catron dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not blockade Southern ports without Congress’ approval.

title: The Founders warned against secret arrests. ICE is testing that principle.
authors: Autumn Billings, Jacob Sullum, Christian Britschgi, Sam Raus, Tosin Akintola, Josh Pauzé
description:
Since the beginning of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown in January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claims more than 1.1 million people have been arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) combined.
It's true that publicly disclosing someone's arrest, particularly a criminal arrest, may damage their reputation.
Trump immigration crackdown has been a source of ongoing debate since its inception.
Since the Founding, Americans have been rightly skeptical of government overreach and the potential to abuse arrest powers.
In the era of Trump's immigration crackdown, this skepticism is even more warranted, and accountability is even more needed.
text:
Since the beginning of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown in January 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claims more than 1.1 million people have been arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) combined. But so far, the names of most arrestees have been kept secret. This lack of public disclosure threatens Americans' ability to hold the government accountable.

While ICE will disclose some details about detainees, the agency's refusal to provide the names, dates of birth, and locations of detainees violates the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), according to a federal lawsuit filed by The Marshall Project on Tuesday. In denying FOIA requests for this information, ICE claims the "privacy interests of the individuals in the records…requested outweigh any minimal public interest disclosure of the information," and revealing such information would "increase the risk of misuse, unwanted contact, harassment, stigma, or other privacy harms," according to the complaint.

A curious position given the DHS' own "worst of the worst" website discloses all kinds of information, including names and photos, while boasting about the detention of select immigration detainees with criminal records.

It's true that publicly disclosing someone's arrest, particularly a criminal arrest, may damage their reputation. But it's a necessary tradeoff to ensure a functioning democracy. Disapproval of anonymized arrests dates back to the Magna Carta. This pro-liberty stance was adopted early in America's Founding. In Federalist No. 84, Alexander Hamilton denounced the "practice of arbitrary imprisonments" as "the favorite and most formidable instruments of tyranny." He went on to cite Sir William Blackstone, an English jurist who greatly influenced America's Founders, quoting: "The confinement of the person, by secretly hurrying him to jail, where his sufferings are unknown or forgotten, is a less public, a less striking, and therefore a more dangerous engine of arbitrary government."

Throughout much of American history, law enforcement agencies have disclosed the identities of those arrested through police blotters and other means in the name of transparency and government accountability. Today, 27 states have codified this practice, according to an amicus brief filed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in a similar but separate case involving ICE's refusal to release the names of those arrested during a 10-day immigration enforcement operation in Chicago. And even when statutes don't plainly state arrest logs qualify as public records, courts have consistently held they do, the ACLU argues. Indeed, the Supreme Court has already ruled that the constitutional right to privacy does not extend to the publication of official acts, such as arrests.

"We are seeking transparency and access to information that have existed within the criminal justice system for centuries," said The Marshall Project's editor in chief, Jennifer Peter. Concealing the names of detainees "makes it far more difficult for their loved ones and attorneys to help them—and for organizations like The Marshall Project to shine a light on what's truly happening within immigration camps," Peter continued.

Trump immigration crackdown has been a source of ongoing debate since its inception. Leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, a recent New York Times poll found that 50 percent of Americans trust the Democratic Party to do a better job of handling immigration, compared to 46 percent trusting Republicans more.

Opponents of Trump's approach to immigration have routinely cited concerns over the use of force, wrongful arrests, detentions, and deportations, including those of U.S. citizens, and the mistreatment of detainees. Proponents of limited government and financial accountability have also raised concerns over the opaque yet explosive expansion of federal agencies, including over $200 billion in funding for FY 2027 and the 100 percent increase in both CBP and ICE funding, reaching nearly 44,000 agents combined, all in the name of immigration enforcement.

Since the Founding, Americans have been rightly skeptical of government overreach and the potential to abuse arrest powers. In the era of Trump's immigration crackdown, this skepticism is even more warranted, and accountability is even more needed.

title: The Trump Administration May Have Just Lied to Judge About an ICE flight to Equatorial Guinea

text:
This is a breaking story and will be updated.

Attorneys asked a judge to bar an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) charter flight from leaving Equatorial Guinea Friday unless their client was onboard in an emergency motion filed shortly after the aircraft landed on the island city of Malabo. An ICE official had told the judge in a sworn statement a day earlier that the flight to Equatorial Guinea had been canceled, a claim the attorneys called “plainly false.”

Flight data indicates the plane took off two hours and 30 minutes later, before the judge issued a ruling.

Earlier this month, Arizona District Court Judge John C. Hinderaker ordered the Trump administration to return Ahmed Soliman—a 31-year-old gay Egyptian national—to the United States, ruling that his due process rights had been violated when he was expelled to Equatorial Guinea, a country he has no ties to, in April. In recent days, Soliman’s attorneys have filed several motions claiming the government was not complying with the order.

In a Wednesday motion, Soliman’s attorneys cited a story from the Prospect, which said documents the Prospect had obtained showed an Eastern Airlines plane chartered by ICE was scheduled to leave Alexandria, Louisiana, the next day, with planned stops in Senegal, Equatorial Guinea, Burundi, and the Central African Republic. The documents also showed the purpose of the flight to Equatorial Guinea was to expel 25 more third-country nationals there, with no stated plan to bring Soliman on board.

But the next day, ICE agent Andrea Chiriboga Villacis told the judge the flight to Equatorial Guinea had been canceled: “On October 22, 2026, ERO headquarters advised that the anticipated third-country removal mission to Equatorial Guinea had been cancelled. Therefore, that mission is not available as a means to transport Petitioner to the United States.”

That does not appear to have been true. Flight data shows the Boeing 767 aircraft landed in Malabo at 4:40 p.m. local time, 11:40 a.m. Eastern time.

“Because Defendants’ attestations were plainly false, Petitioner respectfully requests that the Court enjoin Defendants’ plane from departing Malabo without [Soliman],” the motion said.

Flight data shows the plane has since taken off.

Activists in Louisiana watched from a distance on Thursday as dozens of shackled immigrants were loaded onto the plane at Alexandria International Airport. The plane took off about fours late, according to the documents obtained by the Prospect.

The documents also indicated 25 “detainees” would be expelled in Equatorial Guinea, 30 in Burundi, and 100 in the Central African Republic. All three countries are confirmed third-country removal “hosts” in the Trump administration’s expanding network.

At least 63 third-country nationals have been sent to Equatorial Guinea since last November via at least six ICE-chartered flights, where they have reported being beaten, threatened, held at gunpoint, and deprived of food, water, hygiene products, and medical care. In September, Soliman and another man were disappeared to a local jail for a month, after speaking with the media, including the Prospect, about the latest incident, in which a security officer was caught on video pointing an assault-style rifle at them and another man, while the officer’s supervisor shouted, “Shoot him! Shoot him!”

Soliman was injured in a car accident while he was being returned to the hotel two weeks ago, his lawyers said, and was hospitalized over the weekend due to a serious illness.

Soliman “continues to suffer irreparable harm every day that he remains in Equatorial Guinea,” his attorneys said in the latest filing. “This is the very essence of irreparable harm.”

title: ICE sighting outside Sutter County polling center raises questions about voter intimidation
description:

text:
This story has been updated to include a response from the Department of Homeland Security.

A reported presence of federal immigration officers outside a Northern California elections office is raising concerns about voter intimidation as the Trump administration steps up its scrutiny of voter eligibility.

An observer with immigrant rights group NorCal Resist reported seeing Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers outside the Sutter County Elections Office in Yuba City on Monday.

The sighting was reported the same day the Trump administration announced charges against 28 foreign nationals in California in cases involving alleged election-related crimes, including registering to vote or voting in U.S. elections. Multiple of the individuals arrested were from Northern California including two from Sacramento and one from Vacaville.

Photographs provided by NorCal Resist show an officer with equipment marked ICE and ERO, which stands for Enforcement and Removal Operations. The vehicles were unmarked.

Courtesy of NorCal Resist

NorCal Resist Program Director Giselle Garcia said the officers remained in the parking lot for a little over two hours.

Sutter County Registrar of Voters Donna Johnston said she approached the vehicles but could not identify which agency the officers were with.

“I just let them know that they were in our parking lot and then I gave them our little law enforcement brochures for law enforcement at the polls,” Johnston said.

Johnston said law enforcement vehicles are not unusual at the elections office because it’s near the sheriff’s office. But the sheriff’s office confirmed the officers were not its own.

UC Davis law professor Kevin Johnson said the reported sighting comes amid broader concerns about immigration enforcement and the effect it could have on eligible voters.

He also questioned what role armed immigration officers would have near polling places.

“The burden’s on the federal government to show why armed officers near polling places are necessary at this time,” Johnson said. “It sounds to me like it’s just a political strategy and one that’s going to have costs on particular communities.”

Johnson said the presence of immigration officers at or near polling places could frighten people who worry they might be targeted, including U.S. citizens.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said that claims that ICE targeted a polling location are false.

“ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action,” a spokesperson said in a statement to CapRadio.

Many voters expect immigration enforcement at the polls

Research from the UC San Diego Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections suggests concerns about immigration enforcement at polling places extend beyond Sutter County.

Thad Kousser, co-director for the center and a political science professor at UC San Diego, said election officials began reporting concerns from voters about possible ICE activity at polling places as federal immigration enforcement increased.

A September survey the center conducted found that 40% of respondents nationwide said they expected immigration officers to be present at a voting location in their community.

“And when we ask people, ‘Do you expect that you might face questions, harassment, intimidation even if you’re a U.S. citizen?’ We saw stark differences across racial and ethnic groups,” he said.

Kousser said close to 40% of Asian Americans, about a third of Latinos and a quarter of Black Americans said they did expect this while less than 10% of White Americans did.

The research also found that providing people with information about their voting rights could help ease concerns.

“The important thing is to give voters the information that their state and local election officials are there to ensure that voting laws are protected and their voting rights are upheld and everyone, no matter what their position or party, can have their voice heard in this critical election,” Kousser added.

That same survey also found that fewer than half of Americans expect a free and fair midterm election.

Voters say they won’t be deterred

Some Yuba City voters who spoke with CapRadio after the officers had left said reports of their presence worry them, but wouldn’t keep them from voting.

Daniel Matthews and his brother Lester also had voted at the elections office that day.

“They need to go away,” Daniel said, referring to the ICE officers reportedly seen near the polling location earlier that day.

“It should be addressed,” Lester added.

Mary Page-Molinar voted at the Sutter County Elections Office with her husband, Reynaldo, and said she has become more cautious about how she casts her ballot, preferring to deliver it in person rather than mailing it in.

Gerardo Zavala/CapRadio

She has two relatives who work for ICE, but she said she’s uneasy about the agency’s current operations.

“I feel like a lot of it is they’re just thugs and that’s the way I feel about it,” she said.

The couple said they had not witnessed the reported activity themselves. But Molinar said she would not let concerns about immigration enforcement affect her participation in elections.

“I am not going to let anyone affect my vote,” Page-Molinar added.

text:
Investigation Finds Hundreds of U.S. Citizens Detained by ICE

California officials are calling for an investigation into the actions of federal immigration officers after they allegedly injured and detained a U.S. citizen. Ricardo Gonzalez’s detainment comes as an investigation by ProPublica found that more than 500 citizens have been caught up in the administration’s immigration operations. William Brangham discussed more with ProPublica’s Nicole Foy.

Supreme Court Rejects Trump Policy Restricting Treatment for Transgender Federal Inmates

In a blow to President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court said Wednesday that his administration cannot enforce a new policy that restricts treatment for transgender inmates in federal prison. The justices in a brief order rejected an emergency application filed by the administration that sought to block a lower court injunction against the proposal. The court order included no explanation, saying only that two conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, would have granted it.

Exiled Critic of Rwandan President Found Beheaded in Uganda

An exiled vocal critic of the Rwandan government has been found decapitated near Kampala, south-central Uganda. Robert Kabera, a former major sergeant who fled Rwanda several years ago, was living in Uganda. The former soldier was not critical of the government during his time with the military, but grew increasingly opposed to Rwandan President Paul Kagame. Rwandan authorities have been accused of assassinating opponents of President Kagame, who has governed the country since coming to power in 2000.

Criminal Networks Threaten the Amazon. Indigenous Leaders Want the UN to Act.

Indigenous leaders from across the Amazon are taking their fight against illegal mining, drug trafficking and deforestation to a United Nations conference. More than a dozen Indigenous representatives from Peru, Brazil, Colombia and Ecuador are participating in the U.N. conference on transnational organized crime. The leaders want governments to tackle the financial networks behind environmental crimes while giving Indigenous peoples a greater role in protecting their ancestral territories and shaping a proposed international agreement.

A new lawsuit is challenging the Trump administration’s ability to station federal agents at the polls.

Immigration enforcement should not happen at the polls. That’s the argument of the County Board of Arlington in a new federal lawsuit aimed at keeping ICE agents and the FBI away from voters during the election. Arlington County Board member Susan Cunningham says stationing federal agents at the polls is clearly illegal.

"There is a federal law conveniently called ‘Troops at Polls’ that was passed by Congress in 1865," Cunningham says. "And that addresses the issue very plainly that no armed troops or agents of the federal government are allowed at polling places."

Critics of the lawsuit say federal agents can enforce immigration laws anywhere they want.

"Absent a viable allegation that the ICE agency intends to use illegal intimidation tactics to prevent lawful voting, I don't see how a judge could possibly rule in a county's favor," says legal expert Rich Kelsey.

The lawsuit is asking the federal court to declare Trump administration polling place policies unlawful and enter a declaratory judgement keeping federal immigration enforcement far away from the voting booth.

description:
On July 1, Acacia completed legal orientation and consultation for the mother and child, but failed to file an E28 notice of appearance before the immigration court.
The federal legal services contract with Acacia officially ended July 31.

text:
FIRST ON FOX: A federal timeline provided by officials overseeing unaccompanied migrant children challenges reports that a 1-year-old boy was left to navigate immigration court without counsel, showing that legal service providers intervened to secure representation following an initial hearing.

Addressing media reports highlighting toddlers appearing before immigration judges, Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) Acting Director Angie Salazar and Senior Advisor John Fabbricatore pushed back on headlines alleging systemic gaps in child legal representation, arguing that contractor failures and lack of invoice oversight created the initial court lapses.

"We don't have this big movement where we have a bunch of 1-year-olds who are going to court," Fabbricatore told Fox News Digital.

SEX CRIMINALS, GANG MEMBERS ABUSED CHILD IMMIGRATION PROGRAM TO ENTER US, DHS REVEALS

According to ORR timeline records obtained by Fox News Digital, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers first encountered the 1-year-old boy and his 17-year-old mother near Naco, Arizona, on June 25. The child was accompanied by his mother at all court proceedings.

The critical gap occurred in July under the agency's former contractor, the Acacia Center for Justice, records show.

On July 1, Acacia completed legal orientation and consultation for the mother and child, but failed to file an E28 notice of appearance before the immigration court.

Consequently, during the child's first scheduled court hearing on July 8, no attorney was present — not even as a friend of the court — despite Acacia holding an active federal legal services contract at the time. The federal legal services contract with Acacia officially ended July 31.

FORMER USCIS OFFICIAL, ACCOMPLICE CHARGED IN ALLEGED $960K CITIZENSHIP BRIBERY SCHEME

Following the end of the Acacia contract, the agency transitioned legal service oversight to the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI), which officially initiated legal services Aug. 5. During an Aug. 7 appearance, the mother and child were granted additional time to obtain counsel, while USCRI representatives attended subsequent hearings on Aug. 17 and Aug. 28 as a friend of the court.

On Aug. 31, a motion was filed by the friend of the court and mother requesting court-appointed counsel at government expense, which was later denied by the immigration judge.

Progress continued into September as child advocates were officially appointed on Sept. 23, and USCRI filed a formal E28 notice of appearance on Sept. 25 to become the attorney of record. On Sept. 29, USCRI officially represented both mother and child in immigration court. The judge subsequently granted a continuance on Oct. 2, leading into a follow-up hearing scheduled for Friday.

Officials explained that the July breakdowns highlighted the core reason the administration terminated Acacia's multimillion-dollar contract, which was awarded under the Biden administration in November 2023. According to federal contract records on USAspending.gov, the Department of Health and Human Services had awarded the Acacia Center for Justice a $356.3 million bridge contract for legal services for unaccompanied children. Of that total award, more than $236.9 million had been outlaid prior to the contract's dissolution.

The network previously provided counsel to roughly 20,000 migrant children across the U.S., according to its website.

"I knew we were signing off on every invoice that we were receiving for legal services to the tune of $20-plus million sometimes each month," she told Fox News Digital. "So it made no sense to me that legal service providers were saying kids were unrepresented for a lack of funding."

"I tried to understand who was represented before," she added. "I tried to understand what we were paying for under this direct representation, but the invoices we received were completely redacted. There is no way I could ever know exactly what service was provided during the month."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Acacia Center for Justice for comment. The contract funded a slew of services, including legal screenings, representations and presentations on the rights of migrant children in detention.

Following the dissolution of the Acacia contract, the ORR entered into a $20 million contract with USCRI, which expires Dec. 31.

"So USCRI was showing up in court as a friend of the court to ensure that there was at least somebody present in case Acacia did not show up," Fabbricatore said. "Now, as those cases are being looked at, USCRI is able to go in and actually meet with these children and then represent them in a follow-up hearing. So there may be some hearings where a child shows up, and initially they don't have representation, but USCRI will be there, identify that child, and then be able to move forward in the future as a representative for that child."

WOMAN EXPOSED RUNNING VISA FRAUD SCHEME SPANNING YEARS, POSING AS IMMIGRATION OFFICER

Salazar emphasized that ORR officials track which children are represented by which lawyers on specific dates, noting that the agency respects attorney-client privilege.

"The former provider refused to give us those measurables," Fabbricatore said. "They refused to give us the alien registration number so we could determine what cases they were actually representing. They didn't want to give that. They refused to give that, and that was a holdup for us because we needed to know who was actually being represented so we can ensure that every kid at least had their legal orientation and had a legal representative that was talking to them."

HUNDREDS OF JAILED ILLEGAL ALIENS RELEASED BACK ONTO BLUE-STATE STREETS DESPITE ICE DETAINERS, RECORDS SHOW

Salazar noted that about 2% of migrant children in ORR custody are under the age of 5. Another 85% are ages 13 to 17, with 62% falling into the 16-to-17 bracket.

"What we said to our new grantee (USCRI): ‘We want you in 100% of the hearings where kids in our care are showing up to their immigration hearings,’" she said. "That is happening. I think we're at like 98%."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fabbricatore added there are currently 1,690 migrant children in ORR custody.

"Under Biden, they had 22,000 in care a day. So it's a very vast difference," he said. "We've been able to lower that census, get kids through the court process quicker, and get them back with their parents if possible."

text:
According to friends and family, Roberto Lamour was taken by federal agents inside his own home located at 75 Lenox Road in Flatbush on Oct. 3. Residents inside the building told amNewYork that several ICE agents identified themselves as NYPD officers to gain access to the building and ultimately Lamour’s apartment.

“They accessed the building by saying that they were NYPD, which is a normal occurrence in neighborhoods that are being heavily policed by NYPD. And they were let in, and then at the door they were saying that they were NYPD, that they were looking for some individual, and they were demanding to be let in,” said one resident, who identified herself as Angelina. “They were trying to cooperate, and then when they opened the door, they barged in. They asked for Roberto’s ID, and then they took him.”

Even at that point, Angelina said, Lamour’s wife, Darchnee, still believed that her husband had been arrested by the NYPD and traveled to the local precinct demanding his release. But only after officers at the precinct told her that he wasn’t there did she realize that ICE agents had taken him.

amNewYork reached out to the NYPD for comment and is awaiting a response.

Roberto Lamour is a Haitian immigrant and a father of a 3-year-old daughter. Darchnee Lamour says their daughter regularly despairs over her father’s apprehension.

“She cries for him repeatedly, and whenever the doorbell rings, she runs to the door, believing that her father may have returned home. Seeing our young daughter search for her father and cry for him is heartbreaking. At her young age, she cannot understand why he is no longer at home with us,” Darchnee Lamour said in a statement.

On Oct. 22, residents and elected officials including Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, rallied in support of the Lamours, and demanded Roberto’s immediate release.

Williams charged that the Trump administration’s zero-tolerance immigration crackdown is not about enforcing the law, but rather something far more sinister. He called the president a “grand wizard,” referring to the KKK, and compared the current regime to employing tactics of Nazi Germany.

“There’s a grand wizard in the White House. We are in the Fourth Reich. These are not exaggerations. These are not hyperboles. This is what is happening. Many of us said that this would happen, they are literally making people who were here legally, quote unquote, not here legally anymore,” Williams railed. “I’m going to keep fighting till Roberto comes home.”

Lamour was originally taken to Delany Hall before being transferred to a Detention Center in Mississippi. Friends say he does not have a criminal record.

text:
How can human rights be protected and advanced in an increasingly complex world? That question will guide Human Rights 2026: Current Challenges & Strategies, a two-day conference hosted by the Urban Morgan Institute for Human Rights at the University of Cincinnati Donald P. Klekamp College of Law on Nov. 6–7, 2026.

The free conference will bring together leading scholars, legal practitioners, advocates and members of the university community to examine current human rights challenges and explore strategies for advancing social justice. Through panel discussions, presentations and opportunities for engagement, participants will consider the role of law, policy, advocacy and the arts in addressing issues affecting communities around the world.

“The challenges to the rule of law and human rights are great. We have assembled an extraordinary cast to discuss these challenges, to inspire us to meet these challenges,” said Bert B. Lockwood, Distinguished Service Professor of Law | Director, Urban Morgan Institute.

The conference will open Friday, Nov. 6, with a welcome from UC Klekamp Law Dean Haider Hamoudi, who will address Islamophobia, followed by a fireside chat featuring Harold Hongju Koh, Sterling Professor of International Law at Yale Law School, and Paul Hoffman, a civil and human rights litigator and director of the Defending Democracy Clinic at the University of California, Irvine School of Law.

Their discussion, Challenges & Strategies for Advancement of Human Rights, will explore approaches to protecting human rights through legal advocacy and international law.

Additional Friday sessions will examine immigration and the U.S. government, corporations and human rights, and human trafficking. Presenters include scholars and practitioners whose work spans international law, refugee protection, corporate accountability and human trafficking prevention and advocacy.

Saturday's program will expand the conversation to issues affecting the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersect and asexual community and the relationship between environmental protection and human rights. A panel titled The Art of Judging will feature judges who were fellows of the Urban Morgan Institute, offering perspectives shaped by their experiences in the legal profession and on the bench.

The conference also will examine how creative expression can illuminate human rights issues and deepen public understanding.

A Saturday afternoon panel, Human Rights and the Arts, will explore connections between artistic expression, literature and social justice. The day's programming will culminate in an evening reading of Lemkin's House, a play by award-winning playwright Catherine Filloux, whose work has addressed human rights for decades.

The presentation will feature actors from UC's College Conservatory of Music, bringing an interdisciplinary dimension to the conference and highlighting how the arts can help audiences engage with difficult histories and ongoing human rights concerns.

Founded in 1979, the Urban Morgan Institute for Human Rights was the first endowed institute at an American law school devoted to international human rights law. The institute supports human rights education and experiential learning, connecting students with opportunities to study international human rights law and engage with organizations and practitioners working in the field.

The institute also publishes the Human Rights Quarterly, a multidisciplinary academic journal published by Johns Hopkins University Press and recognized as a leading publication in the field.

By bringing together scholars, practitioners, judges, alumni and students, Human Rights 2026 continues the institute's work of fostering informed discussion and advancing understanding of the legal and practical challenges involved in protecting human rights.

text:
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar will move out of her Washington, D.C., home that federal agents searched last week, she said Wednesday, noting that attention brought on by the raid has made her feel unsafe there.

WATCH: Rep. Omar accuses Trump of political intimidation after agents search her home

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen, said Wednesday in her first interview since the search that she is "confident in the fact that I didn't do anything wrong."

The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.

In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterms, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for reelection in a deep blue district centered in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.

Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.

The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.

Omar came with her family to the U.S. at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a U.S. citizen five years later, in 2000.

"It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I'm sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap," she said in the interview.

The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.

Omar said the agents were "intrusive but polite," logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

Associated Press reporter Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

text:
A British photographer is facing deportation from Sweden and forced separation from his 16-month-old son after authorities ruled in favour of the country’s immigration interests.

Simon Montgomery’s application to remain after the birth of his son last year was rejected on several grounds by Sweden’s migration agency, a decision that was then upheld by the migration court.

He is appealing to the higher migration court, arguing that he has EU freedom of movement rights as his son is a German citizen through his mother. “I am not here because I want to be in Sweden, I am only in Sweden to be with my son,” he said.

The couple separated shortly after the child was born but Montgomery, who grew up without his father in his life, said he was determined to stick around and be there for his newborn.

The pair have legally recognised joint custody, with a parenting agreement that meant his time with his son increased as he got older and no longer needed night-time breastfeeding.

He said he saw his son three days a week and took an active part in his care and daily routine with a “stable parenting plan” agreed via discussions with the municipal family law service.

He moved to Sweden after Brexit so was not entitled to any withdrawal agreement residency rights, but applied to stay on the basis he was the father of an EU citizen.

Montgomery said it was shocking that Sweden was prepared to separate a son from his father, even though the child had rights under EU law as well as international conventions. “Everything in Sweden is about the children’s right to both parents,” Montgomery said.

“But this seems to be ignoring all of that, when it comes around to immigration. Sometimes I feel like people don’t know what happens here. That’s why it’s so important to have these stories told.

“Everyone’s so friendly here; society works and things are nice. And when you tell them what’s happened, they just look shocked. They think you must have done something wrong, and when I explain I have done nothing wrong they just don’t understand.”

Montgomery said he was unable to leave Sweden to see elderly relatives in the UK for fear he would be blocked from returning to be with his son.

“It’s almost like torture in some ways, like having to make these decisions between staying to fulfil your parenting roles and not being able to visit my 98-year-old grandmother back in the UK and say my goodbyes,” he said.

His residency application, made when his son was six months old, was rejected last December by the migration agency on the grounds there was no evidence he had “actual care” for the child, who at that point still stayed overnight with his mother.

It also said he was free to maintain a relationship with his son from afar as he could enter the country visa-free and “still have the opportunity to visit the child in Sweden”.

He appealed against the decision but the court this month sided with the authorities, which assessed, according to the ruling, that the “state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs your interest in the protection of your private and family life in a proportionality assessment”.

Montgomery said he was taken aback by the court’s suggestion he did not need to be in Sweden full-time because he could visit his son by entering the country as a visitor. “Because I can come here visa-free, [they say] it shouldn’t interrupt my parenting ability. That’s crazy because I look after my son three days a week now … and overnights are about to start very soon.”

According to court papers, the decision to reject an application for residency and a simultaneous decision that he should be deported was made “primarily on the grounds that he had not demonstrated that he met the conditions for the right of residence as a family member of an EEA citizen”.

His lawyer argued that if he were “forced to leave Sweden, this would undermine the process and create instability for his son”. They added: “His son is an infant and is in a critical attachment phase where it is in his best interest to have both parents physically present and actively involved.”

They argued that the boy’s father’s presence was “particularly important” because his former German partner did not have a family network to rely on if she was sick or at appointments.

“Deportation would constitute a disproportionate interference in their family life,” they said, arguing that the lower migration court had interpreted “actual care” – evidence of a child’s relationship with a parent – “too narrowly on the grounds that the son primarily lives with his mother”.

They alleged forcibly separating a son from his father would violate article 8 of the European convention of human rights.

Montgomery is appealing against the case to the higher court but said he wanted to share the story so people understood how immigration law was being implemented.

Sweden’s migration agency has been approached for comment. The German government said it could not comment on the case.

text:
A petition calling for the release of Dian Zhao Lin from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention is gaining support in Mount Morris, where community members say the longtime restaurant owner has been part of the community for more than two decades.

Supporters are urging ICE and the Department of Homeland Security to release Lin while his immigration case proceeds through the legal system, according to the petition.

"For more than 20 years, Mr. Lin has called Mount Morris home," the petition states. "He has raised his family here, operated a successful business, contributed to our local economy, and been part of the community we all share."

The Lin family has operated Mun Yuen Chinese Restaurant in Mount Morris since 2005. The family did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What does DHS say about Lin’s immigration case?

The Department of Homeland Security said Lin was apprehended Tuesday during an enforcement operation in Mount Morris, Livingston County. The agency described him as a Chinese national who entered the United States illegally in 1998.

DHS said Lin was also known as Sin Zhao Ling. According to the agency, Lin entered the country illegally in 1998 and was released into the United States by the Clinton administration. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 1999, DHS said.

In July 2023, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied a motion to reopen his case, according to the agency.

DHS said Lin would remain in ICE custody pending removal.

“To be clear: work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States,” the agency said.

Petition highlights Lin’s ties to Mount Morris

“Mr. Lin is not a stranger to Mount Morris. He is our neighbor,” the petition states.

Supporters say Lin’s family ties, history in the community and contributions as a local business owner should be considered as federal authorities review his case.

"After more than 20 years of calling Mount Morris home, Mr. Lin deserves the opportunity to be with his family and have his case heard fairly," the petition states.

Mount Morris mayor expresses support for Lin family

Mayor Kelly Bacon voiced support for the Lin family in a written statement and on her Facebook page.

“Mr. and Mrs. Lin operate a successful Chinese restaurant in our village that has been a cherished part of our local business community for many years,” Bacon said. She described the couple as hardworking, kind and generous neighbors who have raised their children in the community.

“As Mayor, I cannot overstate the positive impact they have had on the life and culture of our small village,” she said, adding that the village would offer support in helping reunite Lin with his family.

Hochul speaks with DHS secretary about detained New Yorkers

Gov. Kathy Hochul said Thursday evening that she had spoken with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin about Lin’s detention and the case of German Machado Guillen, a Venezuelan-born SUNY Brockport employee who was taken into ICE custody the previous week.

Hochul said Machado Guillen was accused of overstaying his authorized stay in the United States by nearly a decade.

“I want their families to know that I’m doing everything in my power to bring their loved ones home,” Hochul said in a social media post. “I’m encouraged by the Secretary’s willingness to engage, and I’ll continue pushing for their swift return.”

title: New York Banned ICE Contracts. Pro-ICE Sheriffs Could Stand in the Way. - Bolts Mag
authors: Daniel Nichanian, Felipe De La Hoz, Alex Burness
description:
Arteta says no longer renting space to ICE in the local jail will hurt the county budget.
Immigrants’ rights groups, meanwhile, say they’re focused on the health and safety of detainees in Orange County.
New York Lawyers for the Public Interest published a report late last year based on reviewing medical records of over a dozen of ICE detainees.
The office of Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
If and when the jail stops housing ICE detainees, that doesn’t end the conversation over immigration detention in the county.
text:
This story is part of Bolts’ series on sheriffs in the run-up to the midterms; read more on Maryland, North Carolina, Washington, and Wisconsin.

When New York legislators approved the state budget earlier this year, they folded in legislation to protect immigrant communities from President Donald Trump’s aggressive crackdown. The legislation, which bars localities from contracting with federal immigration agencies, was a victory for immigrants’ rights advocates but they knew it was only part of the battle; ensuring compliance would be crucial to actually reducing ICE’s presence in the state.

The most visible sort of cooperation that New York barred was participation in the 287(g) program, which effectively deputizes local law enforcement to carry out some of the functions of immigration agents. But lawmakers also restricted county detention contracts, which allow ICE to hold detainees in local jails in exchange for federal money—a practice that exploded last year as ICE arrests surged.

Orange County, a populous community some 30 miles northwest of New York City whose jail had become a sort of waystation in ICE’s national detention network, has quickly become a test of the law’s aftermath.

The jail is run by Sheriff Paul Arteta, a Republican who is holding ICE detainees there in accordance with a contract that the county first entered into in 2008, and that has long drawn scrutiny due to the dismal conditions immigrants have endured. The new state law is forcing Orange County to terminate this relationship, though so far the transfer of immigrant detainees out of the jail has been opaque.

Arteta has resisted the law, joining a group of law enforcement officials to sue over its implementation in late August. The lawsuit also includes sheriffs in counties like Broome that were in the 287(g) program. Now, Arteta and other Republicans are railing against the law as the midterm elections approach. Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the GOP nominee for governor who had joined 287(g) last year, is attacking Governor Kathy Hochul for “making New York less safe.”

ICE cooperation is also an issue in the sheriff’s race between Arteta and Democratic challenger Bernie Rivers, who has criticized the county’s ties with the agency. Arteta says no longer renting space to ICE in the local jail will hurt the county budget.

Immigrants’ rights groups, meanwhile, say they’re focused on the health and safety of detainees in Orange County. This summer, Dignity Not Detention, a statewide coalition that has long advocated for the termination of ICE contracts, began preparing people held in Orange County for transfers and teaching them their rights, said Kate Johnson-Powers, post-release manager at Envision Freedom Fund, an organization that supports immigrants. “But of course, none of us knew what to expect, besides the legal definitions.”

An earlier generation of debates over county detention contracts with ICE—including in neighboring New Jersey during the first Trump administration—pitted advocates who wanted local jails to stop holding people for ICE against people who were typically their allies, immigration public defenders and families of those detained. The latter pointed out that cancelling the contracts would not necessarily mean anyone would be released from detention, but instead merely moved elsewhere, probably much further away in southern states like Louisiana.

But during the second Trump administration, constant transfers have been the norm for ICE.

Observers of the Orange County jail, or OCJ, told Bolts that, starting in early 2025, it became increasingly routine for federal authorities to bring people to Orange County after arresting them in New York City or upstate, but then quickly transfer them out of state while bringing in people from far away.

“We have seen our clients at OCJ get transferred sometimes in batches, sometimes just individually across the country multiple times,” said Rosa Cohen-Cruz, immigration policy director at the Bronx Defenders. “Often during those processes they lose medication, they’ll get to their new facility and won’t have commissary, so won’t be able to make a phone call, they lose property in the transfer.”

The agency is under no legal obligation to hold people near where they were detained or where their attorneys are.

Ben McCoubrey, data and advocacy manager at Envision, has tracked detainees at OCJ using data obtained by the Deportation Data Project as well as Envision’s own information on detainees it’s in touch with. He told Bolts that before the start of the second Trump administration, the jail consistently had 40 to 50 ICE detainees.

He, too, stressed that federal authorities have been cycling people in and out of OCJ quickly. “They started booking tons of people in, transferring a ton of people out to make space, and just continued,” he said. In recent months, the immigrant population has hit a high of around 120 at once, many either recent arrests, recently transferred in, or on their way out.

“I’ve seen guys come in one night, and the next day they’re shipped out,” said Samuel, a former ICE detainee who spent roughly seven months at OCJ, through the end of August (his name was changed to protect his identity, as he has an active immigration case).

While Samuel was able to win release through a habeas petition, most of his fellow detainees have not. “This guy I know got sent to Texas, he got sent with another guy then came back from Texas, then went to Louisiana, came back from Louisiana,” he said. “They don’t explain nothing to you. Besides what your lawyer explained to you and the [immigration judge] explained to you, whether you get denied or post bond, that’s the only information you get to know.”

From his time in the OCJ, he described how corrections personnel kept shortening the time that they would notify detainees that they would be transferred after some started refusing and trying to barricade themselves inside their cells.

Other detainees backed up this account of cyclical transfers. “They’ll take people over to go suffer over there and then bring them back to Orange County, from Pennsylvania and Louisiana,” said Mateo (also a pseudonym), a detainee who was picked up by ICE while going to work in November 2025 and held until this July.

New York City funds public defender organizations to provide legal defense to immigrants arrested in the city—a service that people ICE arrests elsewhere are not entitled to since immigration removal proceedings are civil procedures.

But on occasion, detainees arrested in NYC and brought to OCJ have been moved so quickly that public defense providers do not even become aware they were there until after they’re already out of state, according to local advocates, hampering their ability to actually provide representation.

Most advocates believe this bedlam to be strategic, helping the Trump administration to make what is supposed to be civil, non-punitive detention more punishing and exhausting in a bid to get people to just give up on their cases and accept removal.

Orange County’s jail has been hampered by allegations of poor conditions affecting detainees, particularly those arrested by ICE.

New York Lawyers for the Public Interest published a report late last year based on reviewing medical records of over a dozen of ICE detainees. They alleged a pattern of delayed, inconsistent, and ineffectual medical care at the facility by both corrections staff and outside medical contractors. The sheriff’s office denied the validity of the report without offering specifics, and stressed that many detainees had been accused of “severe crimes.”

Genesis Ramos, the Democratic leader of the county legislature, told Bolts that her office had followed up on these concerns but had not been able to specifically substantiate them. “What we’ve been assured over and over again is that the jail is subject to a lot of scrutiny and different audits, different levels of certification that the jail has to go through,” she said. “As a legislator, we only have but so much authority in terms of the data and operations in the jail.”

Ramos added that she had visited the jail twice during her time as a local legislator, and “never saw anything that was nefarious in nature or that was alarming or concerning per se.” According to Samuel, though, staff would repaint, clean, and provide better food whenever auditors or legislators would visit. Samuel also complains of medical deficiencies. After he was diagnosed with diabetes in jail, he said the food he was served remained the same and his medical appointments kept being delayed; he is now concerned he may have permanent vision problems.

The actual status of the ICE detainee population at the jail remains unclear. Since the law barring local collaboration with ICE went into effect, detainees were transferred out in large numbers, though some were only transferred after the Aug. 25 date at which the county was required to exercise the termination clause of its ICE contract.

A large group of detainees was transferred to the Brooklyn Metropolitan Detention Center, a federal prison, as part of the process to wind down the ICE contract. According to McCoubrey’s tracking, detainees were also sent to the GEO Group-run ICE facility in Jena, Louisiana, which is also where Mahmoud Khalil was held for months; to the deadly Delaney Hall in New Jersey; to the troubled Miami Correctional Facility in Indiana; and to other institutions in Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Texas.

But advocates at Envision and some public defenders say they caught wind of additional book-ins after Aug. 25. Under state law, localities have until Nov. 25 to certify that they are in compliance, though receiving new detainees in that interim period could arguably run afoul of it.

Johnson-Powers, of Envision, said the fund had received a call to its hotline from an ICE detainee at OCJ as late as Sept. 15. The next day, James Potter, the captain of the corrections division at the sheriff’s office, told a meeting of the county legislature’s public safety committee that “the ICE detainee count was 171 for August and as of this morning it was zero,” per meeting minutes. Potter also noted year-to-date “boarder revenue,” i.e., income from renting jail beds to ICE, was $8.13 million.

In response to Bolts’ questions about the current ICE detainee population, transfers, conditions at the jail, and compliance with state law, the sheriff referred all questions to ICE, which did not respond.

The office of Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus also did not respond to multiple requests for comment. A spokesperson for New York Attorney General Letitia James, who has the power to go after jurisdictions in noncompliance, did not address specific questions about Orange County, but clarified that the office views Nov. 25 as the compliance deadline.

If and when the jail stops housing ICE detainees, that doesn’t end the conversation over immigration detention in the county. In late June, Project Salt Box reported that the federal government leased a massive warehouse in Newburgh, a city in Orange County, with some indication that it could be used for ICE detention, including the requirement that it have a sally port large enough for detainee buses and vans.

The prospect has led to significant community pushback this fall.

ICE detention is also a point of contention in November’s sheriff race between Arteta and Rivers, a rematch of the 2022 election in which Arteta easily prevailed.

Rivers, the Democratic challenger, has criticized Arteta for signing on to the lawsuit against the immigration legislation, arguing that the sheriff should keep their focus local: “Orange County residents deserve a Sheriff who is focused on their needs, not one chasing national headlines at the expense of public trust,” he said in a Facebook post in August. He has also warned that the debates are set to continue given the Newburgh warehouse, telling Bolts that immigration detention was a “hot-topic button… with the federal government for the second time looking to purchase or lease facilities here in Orange County to house ICE detainees.”

“I’m not saying the federal government doesn’t have a right to enforce immigration law; they have every right to enforce immigration law, but the way they’re doing it is just wrong,” he added.

Still, he doesn’t see himself as a “standard-bearer” for the anti-ICE movement in the county. “It does come into the political conversation. People want to talk about ICE,” he told Bolts. “I really didn’t want and don’t want to focus the sheriff race totally on what’s going on in ICE.”

Rivers said he would still consider notifying ICE about detainees when appropriate. But he could not immediately say when it would be, telling Bolts he’d look into the laws and regulations when in office. If elected, Rivers also committed to looking into concerns over food and medical care at OCJ, including for people held there on criminal charges.

But Rivers also lamented that the main reaction he was getting from would-be voters was surprise that there was even an election for sheriff, a reality he partly chalked up to the collapse of local media.

Several of the community organizations that participated in the Dignity Not Detention coalition and pushed for the cancellation of the Orange County ICE contract told Bolts that they’re staying out of the race and had no comment on it. Attention now is focused on support for those who are being moved out, including the group sent to Brooklyn MDC, a federal facility housing roughly 1,400 people that was denounced by a judge in 2024 for its “dangerous, barbaric conditions.”

“The levels of security and just degradation and lack of humanity through this intense security, it’s just very different from being in a small county jail,” said Johnson-Powers.

Still, even if the closure of OCJ to ICE detainees won’t address the broader issues of an administration committed to mass deportation and armed with enormous funding, advocates say the law restricting local cooperation with ICE and the contract’s cancellation have value.

McCoubrey, the advocate at Envision, stresses “the multiplier effect that every ICE bed has,” telling Bolts, “70,000 [total detention] beds is already a scary number. But the fact that that facilitates hundreds and hundreds of thousands of deportations every year really brings home the value of any amount of any dent that you can make in local detention capacity.”
